articles.title: Descubre quién accede a tu cuenta de Google y cómo cerrar sesiones en dispositivos no autorizados
articles.text:
La seguridad de tu cuenta de Google es fundamental en la vida digital actual, donde un solo acceso no autorizado puede exponer correos, archivos, contactos y datos personales. Por eso, saber exactamente en qué dispositivos has iniciado sesión y cómo cerrar sesiones sospechosas es clave para proteger tu privacidad y evitar riesgos innecesarios.
Hoy, con el auge del teletrabajo, el uso compartido de computadoras y la sincronización automática de apps, es fácil perder el control sobre dónde está activa tu cuenta. Aquí te explicamos cómo descubrir quién accede a tu Google y cómo revocar el acceso a dispositivos no autorizados paso a paso.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo ver los dispositivos conectados a tu cuenta de Google
Google facilita la revisión de dispositivos conectados desde la página (google.com/devices). Este panel te permite ver todos los dispositivos, teléfonos, computadoras, tablets, en los que tu cuenta ha estado activa durante las últimas semanas.
Pasos para revisar los dispositivos:
- Accede a tu Cuenta de Google.
- Ve a la sección Seguridad y acceso.
- En el panel Tus dispositivos, selecciona Administrar todos los dispositivos.
- Aparecerá una lista con todos los dispositivos y sesiones recientes, incluyendo la ubicación, el tipo de dispositivo y la última hora de actividad.
Si ves dispositivos o ubicaciones que no reconoces, es posible que alguien más esté usando tu cuenta.
¿Por qué importa saber quién accede a tu cuenta de Google?
Cada vez que inicias sesión en un nuevo dispositivo, navegador o aplicación, se crea una sesión vinculada a tu cuenta de Google. Si olvidas cerrar la sesión en un ordenador público, prestas tu teléfono o pierdes un dispositivo, alguien podría acceder a tu correo, tus archivos de Drive o tus fotos de Google sin tu permiso.
PUBLICIDAD
Además, los ciberdelincuentes pueden intentar ingresar a tu cuenta desde ubicaciones remotas si logran obtener tu contraseña. Revisar regularmente los dispositivos y sesiones activas es fundamental para detectar accesos sospechosos y cerrar cualquier puerta abierta a tu información.
¿Qué es una sesión y por qué aparecen duplicadas?
Una sesión es el periodo en el que tu cuenta de Google está activa en un navegador, aplicación o servicio en un dispositivo específico. A veces verás varias sesiones con el mismo nombre de dispositivo porque:
PUBLICIDAD
- Has iniciado sesión varias veces en el mismo equipo.
- Usaste diferentes navegadores o apps.
- Accediste en modo incógnito o privado.
- Otorgaste acceso a apps de terceros.
Revisa los detalles y, si tienes dudas, cierra todas las sesiones relacionadas para asegurarte de que nadie más pueda acceder.
Cómo cerrar la sesión en dispositivos no autorizados
Si detectas un dispositivo desconocido o uno que ya no usas, es importante cerrar la sesión de inmediato:
- Desde el panel de Tus dispositivos, selecciona el dispositivo sospechoso.
- Haz clic en Salir o Quitar acceso.
- Confirma la acción para revocar el acceso.
Repite el proceso para cada sesión sospechosa. Así, tu cuenta quedará protegida y cualquier intento de acceso requerirá la contraseña nuevamente.
Qué hacer si ves actividad sospechosa
Si detectas un dispositivo nuevo, una ubicación extraña o una hora de uso que no recuerdas, sigue estos pasos:
- Cambia tu contraseña de Google inmediatamente.
- Revisa los permisos de apps de terceros vinculadas a tu cuenta y revoca el acceso a las que no reconozcas.
- Habilita la verificación en dos pasos para añadir una capa extra de seguridad.
- Consulta el historial de actividad y busca accesos inusuales.
Recuerda que a veces puedes ver ubicaciones cercanas (como aeropuertos o ciudades donde viajaste) o sesiones creadas por la sincronización automática de apps, lo que puede causar confusión. Si tienes dudas, es mejor cerrar todas las sesiones desconocidas.
PUBLICIDAD
Consejos para mantener tu cuenta segura
- Usa contraseñas robustas y únicas que no reutilices en otros servicios.
- Activa la verificación en dos pasos.
- No dejes la sesión abierta en computadoras públicas o de otras personas.
- Revisa tu panel de dispositivos al menos una vez al mes.
Controlar quién accede a tu cuenta de Google es una responsabilidad clave en la era digital. Unos minutos de revisión pueden evitar fraudes, pérdidas de información o accesos no autorizados. Mantener tus sesiones bajo control es una forma efectiva de proteger tu identidad y tu información más valiosa en la nube.

articles.title: I hit 40 and knew my lifestyle had to change. This app is helping me power up, take more steps, and supercharge my water intake
articles.text:
I hit 40 and knew my lifestyle had to change. This app is helping me power up, take more steps, and supercharge my water intake
Homescreen Heroes: GO Club helps you make simple health improvements that are actually achievable
I never cease to be amazed at the effectiveness of small habits. Standing up and moving every hour. Drinking small sips of water regularly. Leaving your phone downstairs when you go to bed. Flossing straight after brushing. Giving thanks for one thing as soon as your head hits the pillow.
They seem small and insignificant. Can habits like these really make a difference? In my experience, yes, and James Clear, author of Atomic Habits, agrees. The reality is that each habit may not seem like a big deal, but when combined and performed over time, they can lead to massive changes.
One app that has helped me build and cement new habits in the area of health and fitness is GO Club. This beautifully designed app is the epitome of simplicity. It may only perform a few simple functions, but what it does, it does incredibly well. Over the past few weeks, I’ve grown to love it and have come to rely on its phone widget to keep me moving towards my goals.
This is part of a regular series of articles exploring the apps that we couldn't live without. Read them all here.
At the heart of GO Club is a tracker that measures steps and water intake. Beyond this, it offers reminders and rewards to help you prioritize these small but important habits. Since its launch just 18 months ago, the app has been downloaded by more than 150,000 people and was a finalist in the 2025 App Store Awards.
Hitting your step goal
Increasing the number of steps you take each day sounds simple. All you have to do is put one step in front of another, and the numbers will take care of themselves. I thought the same until I started tracking my progress. Despite setting a goal of 10,000 steps per day, I was regularly only taking between five and six thousand. That surprised me.
The GO Club app not only informed me of my subpar number of steps but also provided all the motivation I needed to do something about it, and it was simpler than I expected.
The simple, no-fuss readout of the number of steps I took that day proved sufficient motivation, and seeing it in the widget every time I unlocked my phone was an easy reminder. GO Club calls this “Steps, without the noise."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Underneath the step count are three other stats presented in small text. These are distance, calories burned, and floors climbed. I didn’t use these, but if you were training to walk a set distance or needed a crude summary of how many calories you were burning each day, I could imagine it proving useful. Beyond this is a chart that displays progress over time so you can make sure you’re moving in the right direction.
The importance of drinking enough water
Step count is recorded automatically, but you enter water intake manually. There’s no way around this because your smartphone or smartwatch simply can’t track how much water you’re drinking. Thankfully, entering the amount of water consumed each day is incredibly straightforward.
To enter an amount, you adjust the slider value and click 'Add.' The app then subtracts this from your goal, 2.5 liters by default, and updates the water bottle graphic for a visual representation of how much water you have left to drink within that day. It’s a strikingly simple graphic that genuinely makes me want to drink water every time I look at it.
Smartwatch integration and a GO Plus subscription
Not everyone will want to rely on a smartphone app or widget to change their step and drinking habits. That’s why GO Club developed a dedicated Apple Watch app so you can glance at your smartwatch to see your progress. The Apple Watch app follows the same design principles as the smartphone app with a strikingly simple and visually appealing layout.
GO Plus lets you get the most from the app. This includes home screen and lock screen widgets, focus mode themes, smart walking plans, Apple Watch widgets, golden hour time slots, and a health trends summary. All of this costs an annual sum of $19.99 / £17.99 or $3.99 / £2.99 per month if you’d prefer a rolling subscription.
Download the GO Club app on iOS.

And of course you can also follow TechRadar on TikTok for news, reviews, unboxings in video form, and get regular updates from us on WhatsApp too.
Writer, app-hoarder, and professional "low battery" enthusiast. Paul spends his days testing wearables so you don’t have to, and his nights wondering if his sleep tracker is judging him. He’s fascinated by the tech that claims to make us better humans—and if it’s wearable, downloadable, or requires a firmware update, he has thoughts on it.
With over 20 years of experience and a first-class Computer Science degree, Paul has navigated the front lines of the tech and creative industries. His work has been published internationally and appears regularly in Digital Camera World and Creative Bloq.

articles.title: Mac Mini und Mac Studio: Warum du noch Wochen auf deinen neuen Computer warten musst
articles.text:
Mac Mini und Mac Studio: Warum du noch Wochen auf deinen neuen Computer warten musst
Apple hat den eigenen Erfolg unterschätzt: Der Konzern passt sich noch immer an die ungewohnt hohe Nachfrage nach Macs für KI-Anwendungen an. Das berichtet der IT-Newsdienst The Information unter Berufung auf informierte Kreise. Hintergrund ist der Trend zu lokalen KI-Systemen. Die Modelle werden immer leistungsfähiger, viele sind quelloffen oder kommen mit offenen Gewichten – also frei verfügbaren Modelldaten, die jeder auf eigener Hardware nutzen kann. Nutzer:innen brauchen dafür weder ein Abo noch müssen sie steigende Token-Kosten zahlen. Spätestens mit der Welle lokaler KI-Agenten wie OpenClaw setzte ein Boom bei Apple-Rechnern ein, die vergleichsweise günstig sind und sich dank schneller M-Chips gut für KI eignen.
Wochenlange Wartezeiten bei neuen Modellen
Sichtbar wird der Engpass bei den neuen Mac Minis mit M5 Pro und M6 sowie bei den Mac Studios mit M5 Max und M5 Ultra. Apple hat die Geräte angekündigt, liefert sie aber erst Wochen später aus. Für die Top-Variante des Mac Studio M5 Ultra mit 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher nennt der Konzern nicht einmal einen Preis – vor Oktober dürfte sie nicht erscheinen. Dass Apple die Geräte ungewöhnlicherweise schon im August vorgestellt hat, führt The Information ebenfalls auf den KI-Boom zurück. KI-Labore und KI-Cloud-Anbieter kauften die Rechner demnach „in LKW-Ladungen“.
Bereits im Juni soll Apple ein Event unter dem Namen „Business at the Park“ ausgerichtet haben. Neben Altchef Tim Cook und Nachfolger John Ternus waren dem Bericht zufolge hochrangige Mitarbeiter von Anthropic, Disney und Ford vor Ort. Apple habe dort dafür geworben, KI-Anwendungen lieber lokal als im Rechenzentrum zu betreiben. Im Mittelpunkt stand laut The Information der Mac Mini. Firmen wie OpenAI sollen „Zehntausende“ Mac Minis und Mac Studios gekauft haben – für Reinforcement Learning, also das Training von Modellen durch Belohnungssignale. Anthropic mietet Mac Minis bei Amazon Web Services. Erste Anbieter kaufen zudem große Mengen Apple-Hardware für eigene „Neoclouds“: Sie stellen die Rechner in ihre Rechenzentren und vermieten die dort laufenden KI-Anwendungen weiter.
Nvidia könnte profitieren
Apple wirbt also für lokale KI, kann aber nicht schnell genug liefern. Schuld ist die Krise bei Arbeitsspeicher und SSDs: Die Speicherchips für die M-Prozessoren sind teuer und kaum zu bekommen – selbst für einen Großkunden wie Apple. KI-Chip-Hersteller wie Nvidia nehmen noch größere Mengen ab.
„Wenn Firmen nicht in der Lage sind, ihre Macs zu bekommen, migrieren sie auf andere Hardware-Möglichkeiten“, zitiert The Information den Chef von webAI, einem Unternehmen, das Apple-basierte KI-Werkzeuge an Firmen verkauft. Nvidia versucht, diese Lücke mit eigenen lokalen KI-Rechnern wie dem DGX Spark zu füllen.

articles.title: En 1993, un surcoreano entró en Japón con el pasaporte de su hermano. 33 años después, Japón acaba de descubrir hasta dónde llegó la visa de 15 días
articles.text:
Mun Jong-gi llegó a Japón desde Corea del Sur con una autorización para permanecer apenas 15 días. Según la policía japonesa, había utilizado el pasaporte de su hermano menor y buscaba algo bastante concreto: empleos mejor pagados que los que podía conseguir en su país. El hombre no regresó cuando venció el permiso. De hecho, 33 años después, una información recibida por la policía descubrió hasta dónde habían llegado aquellos 15 días.
De 15 días a 33 años. Mun Jong-gi tenía 39 años cuando llegó a Japón en septiembre de 1993 y recibió permiso para permanecer en el país durante únicamente 15 días. La policía. como decíamos, sostiene que entró utilizando el pasaporte de su hermano menor y que su intención era encontrar trabajos que le permitieran ganar más dinero que en Corea del Sur.
Ocurre que cuando terminó aquel plazo no regresó: al contrario, permaneció en Japón y, según las investigaciones, continuó viviendo allí prácticamente de manera ininterrumpida hasta 2026.
No es solo cuánto tiempo, sino cómo lo hizo. Durante esas más de tres décadas, Mun habría sobrevivido realizando trabajos por días y otros empleos ocasionales, aunque las informaciones disponibles no explican quién lo contrataba ni cómo resolvió durante tanto tiempo otros aspectos cotidianos que normalmente requieren documentación en la nación nipona.
Tampoco existe por ahora una explicación completa de cómo consiguió permanecer tantos años sin que su situación migratoria desembocara antes en una detención. Lo que sí sabemos es que no fue una investigación iniciada en los años noventa la que finalmente permitió encontrarlo: su caso apareció ante la policía más de tres décadas después de su llegada.
La pista. La secuencia que acabó con su vida clandestina comenzó en junio de 2026, cuando la policía recibió información sobre una persona que presuntamente residía ilegalmente en Japón. La Policía de la Prefectura de Shizuoka abrió entonces una investigación que terminó conduciendo hasta Mun en Yaizu, una ciudad costera situada al suroeste de Tokio.
Finalmente fue detenido el pasado 26 de agosto de 2026, con 72 años. Durante el interrogatorio habría reconocido las acusaciones y explicado que había ido encadenando trabajos ocasionales durante su estancia.
La paradoja. La diferencia se debe a una peculiaridad jurídica importante para entender el caso. Aunque su autorización de 15 días expiró en 1993, las informaciones japonesas señalan que la permanencia irregular pasó a ser específicamente castigada penalmente tras un cambio legislativo que entró en vigor en febrero de 2000.
Por eso la policía sitúa el periodo objeto de la acusación desde ese momento: Mun habría permanecido irregularmente en Japón durante casi 33 años, pero la infracción penal que sustenta su arresto comprende aproximadamente los últimos 26.
300.000 casos similares. Mun desembarcó además en un Japón muy diferente al actual en materia migratoria. En 1993, precisamente el año de su llegada, el país contabilizaba 298.646 extranjeros que habían superado el periodo de estancia autorizado, una cifra récord y más de cuatro veces superior a la actual.
En enero de 2026 quedaban registrados 68.488, de modo que su historia comenzó en el momento de máxima expansión del fenómeno y terminó cuando Japón había conseguido reducirlo drásticamente.
La búsqueda de un mejor sueldo. La motivación que Mun habría explicado a los investigadores resulta mucho más convencional y simple que la extraordinaria duración de su estancia: el hombre había viajado a Japón porque esperaba ganar más dinero trabajando allí.
Lo excepcional es que aquella decisión temporal tomada a finales de 1993 acabara prolongándose durante aproximadamente 12.000 días, hasta convertir una autorización de dos semanas en prácticamente media vida. Tenía unos 39 años cuando entró y 72 cuando la policía llamó finalmente a su puerta.
La pregunta más difícil. En estos momentos, la investigación continúa precisamente porque todavía faltan piezas importantes para reconstruir esas tres décadas: cómo consiguió trabajar, qué documentación empleó durante esos años o qué mecanismos le permitieron desarrollar su vida diaria sin residencia legal.
Plus: tampoco se había comunicado todavía una sentencia definitiva ni una decisión final sobre su posible deportación a Corea del Sur. Lo único cerrado en estos momentos es la extraordinaria cronología: Japón le permitió entrar durante dos semanas en septiembre de 1993 y no descubrió su prolongadísima estancia hasta el verano de 2026.

articles.title: GTA VI Extended Gameplay Preview Attracted Over 4 Million Live Viewers
articles.text:
Sunday, August 30th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
GTA VI Extended Gameplay Preview Attracted Over 4 Million Live Viewers
It's been known since Rockstar released the first trailer for GTA VI that the upcoming action game would have a massive impact on the gaming industry, and analysts have predicted week-one sales of $4.5 billion when the game launches in November. Following Rockstar's GTA VI showcase at Gamescom, reports have emerged that, between Netflix, YouTube, and Twitch, nearly 4 million users tuned into the live show—a number that had ripple effects across the internet. 
For starters, in the two days since the GTA VI Extended Look video launched on YouTube, it has racked up over 14 million views, while Streams Charts, a tracker for Twitch stream data, reported 3,970,738 peak stream viewers of the Extended Gameplay stream across both the official and unofficial commentary live streams and watch parties for the three hours it tracked viewership.
		
		Sources:
				Streams Charts, 				via Eurogamer			
	
	
	
		
	
		
For starters, in the two days since the GTA VI Extended Look video launched on YouTube, it has racked up over 14 million views, while Streams Charts, a tracker for Twitch stream data, reported 3,970,738 peak stream viewers of the Extended Gameplay stream across both the official and unofficial commentary live streams and watch parties for the three hours it tracked viewership.
Netflix and Twitch users reported issues logging into their respective platforms due to increased traffic, while Cloudflare claims that Netflix saw 16% increased traffic during the event, and Twitch and YouTube saw a respective 12% and 39% traffic increase. The latter was likely at least partially due to how ubiquitous YouTube embeds are in news reports and official publisher websites, since Rockstar's own website saw a global traffic increase of 172% following the trailer's launch.

articles.title: Key Nvidia and Intel supplier raided over alleged China origin fraud — Unimicron faces probe over PCB origin washing, risk of 40% U.S. tariff penalty
articles.text:
Key Nvidia and Intel supplier raided over alleged China origin fraud — Unimicron faces probe over PCB origin washing, risk of 40% U.S. tariff penalty
Suspects have been released on bail pending investigation.
Taiwanese prosecutors are investigating Unimicron, one of the world’s largest PCB and chip substrate makers and a key supplier to Nvidia, Intel, Google, and Amazon, over allegations that it shipped China-made PCBs back to Taiwan and relabeled them as Taiwanese products, according to Nikkei Asia. Investigators raided the company’s headquarters in Taoyuan’s Guishan District and a manufacturing plant in Zhongli District on August 28, questioning 14 employees as suspects — including the general and deputy general managers of its PCB business — and four more people as witnesses.
Prosecutors say that the alleged conduct contravened Articles 216, 210, and 255 of Taiwan’s Criminal Code, which cover the use of forged private documents and false labeling of an item’s origin. Wang, the person identified as the PCB department general manager, was released on bail of NT$15 million (roughly $473,000), while a deputy general manager identified as Wu was released on NT$12 million (roughly $378,000).
Three others are said to have posted bail ranging from NT$300,000 to NT$5 million, and the remaining nine were released without bail. "There was strong suspicion that they had violated Taiwan's law covering the use of forged private documents and false labeling of goods," the Taoyuan District Prosecutors Office said in a statement. Unimicron told the Taiwan stock exchange that it’s fully cooperating with the investigation and that it doesn’t expect a material impact on its operations.
Since August last year, U.S. Customs and Border Protection has applied an additional 40% tariff on goods that it determines were transshipped through third countries to evade duties, on top of any other applicable penalties, and the agency has no authority to waive or otherwise mitigate the charge. If any relabeled Unimicron PCBs were to reach the U.S., that penalty would fall on the company’s American customers as importers of record.
The White House has identified 40 countries and territories that it says pose an elevated risk of illegal transshipment, with Taiwan flagged as a key concern. Taipei has been running major crackdowns on “origin washing,” where companies claim goods are made in Taiwan to obtain preferential tariff treatment, a crackdown that’s perhaps perfectly illustrated by the fact that prosecutors published names and bail amounts within 24 hours of raiding one of the country’s most important listed tech companies. After all, the “Made in Taiwan” label is ultimately a trade asset whose value rests on the fact that it’s not “Made in China.” Since its elevated risk designation, Taiwan is understandably keen to show Washington that it polices the difference itself rather than leaving it to U.S. Customs.
The products involved in this crackdown appear to be conventional PCBs, not the high-end ABF substrates used for Intel’s EMIB-T platform or Nvidia’s advanced data center accelerators. Unimicron’s offshore manufacturing remains in China for standard substrates, PCBs, HDI, and flexible boards, while its advanced CoWoS-related substrate capacity is based at its Yangmei factory in Taoyuan.
If the case concerns relabeling on individual products, the fallout will be limited to the Taiwanese prosecution. If, however, it turns out that China-made goods were transshipped through Taiwan to alter their origin before export to the U.S., that’s an entirely different story and could trigger CBP’s 40% transshipment penalty on the affected goods, along with potential retroactive duty reassessments, which would hit Unimicron’s American customers as importers of record.

articles.title: China's CXMT beats Western chipmakers to announcement of LPDDR6 mass production — Xiaomi smartphones to debut industry’s first LPDDR6 chips
articles.text:
China's CXMT beats Western chipmakers to announcement of LPDDR6 mass production — Xiaomi smartphones to debut industry’s first LPDDR6 chips
LPDDR6 arrives in less than a year after CXMT started mass-producing LPDDR5.
ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has announced in a social media post that it has started mass production of LPDDR6 memory for a Xiaomi smartphone, Reuters reports. This is not entirely unexpected given the general LPDDR6 mass-production timeline, but the announcement is still surprising because two China-based companies are ahead of industry announcements. Yet, there are caveats.
LPDDR6 is perhaps the most substantial upgrade to the GDDR-class memory ever. Firstly, it uses PAM3 signaling, which encodes 3 bits of information across two symbols, compared with the NRZ signaling used by LPDDR5/LPDDR5X. Second, the data transfer rate increases to 43.2 GT/s. Third, the reduced I/O width from 32 bits to 24 bits requires rework at both the hardware and software levels.
Given the differences between LPDDR5 and LPDDR6, the most important factor here is not exactly LPDDR6 manufacturing, but a broader view.
On the one hand, CXMT reached mass production of LPDDR6 roughly at the same time as the established DRAM leaders, meaning it is on par with them, if not ahead. This marks a substantial change from earlier generations, when Chinese DRAM technology generally lagged considerably behind Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron.
On the other hand, reaching mass production does not necessarily mean that CXMT has achieved full technological or manufacturing parity with its larger rivals. The official announcement covers only one smartphone maker and one model, meaning CXMT's LPDD6 still has to pass validation for other handsets and other makers.
Still, the significance of CXMT's announcement is hard to understate. CXMT is no longer merely catching up by introducing a new memory generation years after its international competitors. With LPDDR6, CXMT is entering the market during the standard's initial commercialization, which means the technology gap between China's leading DRAM producer and the industry's established players has narrowed considerably.
Which brings us to the question of whether CXMT can maintain this pace. Developing a competitive LPDDR6 device is one thing, producing it at high yields and in sufficient volumes to supply major customers is another. For now, we are talking about a niche smartphone with memory operating at undisclosed performance.

If CXMT can mass-produce LPDDR6 for the whole market and manufacturers, we may well have seen the change of the industry leader. Yet, given one niche device, we certainly cannot say so for now.

articles.title: Box-office : la surprise Coyote vs. Acme enfonce Ridley Scott, Spider-Man surpasse Avatar 2
articles.text:
Box-office : la surprise Coyote vs. Acme enfonce Ridley Scott, Spider-Man surpasse Avatar 2
Spider-Man : Brand New Day conserve sa couronne au box-office et se rapproche à grands pas du record américain du film Star Wars Le Réveil de la Force. Sauvé par les fans, le film Coyote vs. Acme démarre bien.
Sorti il y a plus d'un mois maintenant, Spider-Man : Brand New Day reste au sommet du box-office pour la 5ème semaine consécutive et n'est plus loin du plus gros succès américain de tous les temps détenu par Star Wars, épisode VII : Le Réveil de la Force. La nouveauté Coyote vs. Acme signe elle un lancement solide. On fait le point.
Les 900 millions pour Spidey
Avec 22,2 millions de dollars engrangés, l'indéboulonnable Spider-Man : Brand New Day reste le film le plus populaire du week-end au box-office US, loin devant les nouveautés. Le film Sony / Marvel porte ainsi son cumul domestique à 891,5 millions de dollars et s'apprête à devenir le deuxième film à passer la barre hallucinante des 900 millions.
La dernière aventure de l'homme-araignée n'a plus que Le Réveil de la Force (936,6 millions de dollars) devant elle avant de devenir le plus gros succès de tous les temps sur le sol américain, sans prendre en compte l'inflation bien sûr. Une prouesse que le long-métrage devrait atteindre d'ici une petite dizaine de jours.
Brand New Day cumule 2,332 milliards de dollars à l'international et aura dépasser le score global d'Avatar : La Voie de l'eau (2,334 milliards) à l'heure où on écrit ces lignes. S'il devient ainsi le troisième plus gros succès de tous les temps dans le monde, il aura du mal à aller chercher Avengers : Endgame (2,8 milliards) et Avatar (2,923 milliards) plus haut dans le classement. Sony et Marvel ne doivent pas être malheureux pour autant.
Ce week-end a surtout vu la sortie du film hybride Coyote vs. Acme, mêlant animation et prises de vues réelles. Le long-métrage, que Warner Bros. comptait enterrer pour bénéficier de réductions d'impôts (à l'instar de Batgirl), a été sauvé par les fans. En effet, sous la pression populaire, le studio a cédé la distribution à la société indépendante Ketchup Entertainment qui a sorti Coyote vs. Acme sur 3 575 écrans aux États-Unis.
Résultat : 15,4 millions de dollars pour son premier week-end. Un score modeste mais solide vu la taille du film (50 millions de budget) et son marketing réduit. Il faudra attendre de voir si cela se confirme en deuxième semaine, mais le bouche-à-oreille peut faire des merveilles, et l'accueil critique et public et jusque-là très bon. Mauvaise nouvelle pour nous : le film ne devrait pas sortir au cinéma en France.
La performance de Coyote vs. Acme est encore plus notable quand on la compare à l'autre nouveauté du week-end, The Dog Stars. Le film de Ridley Scott avec Jacob Elordi, dôté d'un confortable buget de 70 millions de dollars et d'une belle campagne marketing, fait lui un bide avec seulement 8 millions engrangés pour ses débuts.
Après l'échec relatif de Gladiator 2, et ceux plus lourds de Napoléon et Le Dernier Duel, c'est une nouvelle déconvenue pour le réalisateur d'Alien et Blade Runner. Mais à 88 ans, pas sûr qu'il en est réellement quelque chose à faire. Les financiers de 20th Century Studios et Scott Free Productions sont sans doute un peu moins ravis.

articles.title: "Repousser les limites de la découverte" : les images spectaculaires du lancement du télescope Roman
articles.text:
C’est fait : le télescope Nancy Grace Roman s’est envolé ce dimanche 30 août à bord d’une surpuissante fusée Falcon Heavy. Retour en images sur un lancement voué à révolutionner notre compréhension de l’Univers.
Le rendez-vous était donné à 7h26 heure locale, soit 13h26 en France métropolitaine, depuis le pas de tir historique LC-39A du Centre spatial Kennedy. Et cette fois, il n’y a eu aucun contretemps : la fusée Falcon Heavy de SpaceX, du haut de ses trois boosters, a décollé pile à l’heure prévue. Un lancement qui vient couronner plus d’une décennie de développement, pour un bijou de technologie à 4,3 milliards de dollars.
Un lancement sans accroc
Et le spectacle a été au rendez-vous. Les 21 moteurs Merlin 1D du Falcon Heavy ont rugi puis, 2 minutes 30 après le lancement, ses deux boosters latéraux se sont détachés pour amorcer leur retour vers la Terre avant d’atterrir en douceur à Cape Canaveral. Des images sensationnelles, comme à chaque fois.
Le reste de la mission s’est déroulé sans accroc. Le télescope s’est en effet séparé de l’étage supérieur 31 minutes après le décollage, sous les applaudissements des équipes au sol. Le centre de contrôle de la NASA, situé au Goddard Space Flight Center dans l’État du Maryland, a reçu ses premiers signaux 7 minutes après le lancement, avant de confirmer le déploiement des panneaux solaires du Nancy Grace Roman, en hommage à la première cheffe de l’astronomie à la NASA, un peu plus d’une heure plus tard.
De quoi arracher quelques larmes à Nicky Fox, responsable scientifique de la NASA, visiblement submergée par l’émotion. « Désormais, Roman va nous offrir un nouvel atlas de l’univers, repousser les limites de la découverte et nous montrer ce qui est possible », s’est félicité Jared Isaacman, administrateur de l’agence spatiale.
Il a même reçu un appel téléphonique de Donald Trump en pleine conférence de presse. Le président américain a félicité le dirigeant, bien qu’il ait envisagé, en 2025, de mettre fin au programme du Nancy Grace Roman.
À la recherche de la matière noire
Mais le télescope a encore un long chemin. Direction, à présent, le point Lagrange L2, à environ 1,6 million de kilomètres de la Terre, là où orbite déjà le James-Webb. Un trajet qui doit durer plus de 3 mois, avec une première phase d’une quarantaine de jours consacrée à la mise en route et aux vérifications des instruments.
Une fois sur place, l’engin entrera clairement dans le vif du sujet : percer les mystères de la matière et de l’énergie noires, qui composent l’essentiel de l’Univers sans jamais avoir été observées directement. Il partira, en outre, à la chasse aux exoplanètes grâce à son coronographe de pointe. Un travail que le télescope pourra mener à une vitesse inédite, car il scannera le ciel jusqu’à 1 000 fois plus rapidement que Hubble. Ses premières images sont attendues courant 2027.

articles.title: Le nouvel iPad mini arrive avec ces 4 nouveautés
articles.text:
Privé d’un passage sur scène lors de la keynote Apple du 9 septembre prochain, qui sera dédiée aux iPhone 18 Pro et au très attendu iPhone Ultra pliable, l’iPad mini 8 suivrait sa propre feuille de route. Apple devrait organiser son lancement séparément en octobre, par communiqué de presse ou à l’occasion d’une nouvelle conférence.
Un nouvel iPad mini plus puissant et plus résistant
Ce modèle marquera la première mise à jour de la gamme depuis deux ans, le dernier rafraîchissement remontant à octobre 2024 avec l’arrivée de la puce A17 Pro et la compatibilité avec Apple Intelligence pour l’iPad mini 7. Pour cette nouvelle génération, le constructeur intègrerait un écran OLED et une puce A19 Pro ou A20 Pro. La partie sonore évoluerait elle aussi vers une technologie basée sur les vibrations pour lui donner plus de coffre.
Apple pourrait également en profiter pour changer le design de sa petite tablette et la rendre résistante à l’eau et à la poussière avec une certification IP. Reste maintenant à savoir dans quelle mesure ces modifications impacteront le prix de l’appareil. L’iPad mini 7 est vendu sur le site d’Apple au prix conseillé de 689 € (609 € au lancement). La crise de la mémoire et la montée en gamme pourraient donc se solder par une facture encore plus salée pour le prochain modèle.
L’ombre de l’iPhone Ultra sur le petit format d’Apple
Mais l’arrivée sur le marché de l’iPhone Ultra pourrait redistribuer les cartes pour la plus petite des tablettes de la marque à la pomme. Le futur smartphone pliant d’Apple devrait proposer un format 2-en-1, à mi-chemin entre un iPhone et une petite tablette comme l’iPad mini. On peut donc légitimement se poser la question de la cannibalisation entre les deux produits, même si l’iPhone Ultra sera certainement beaucoup plus cher que la future tablette.
Mais garder au catalogue l’iPad mini peut également faire sens pour les utilisateurs attachés à la séparation entre leur téléphone et leur tablette. La réponse se jouera dans les rayons d’ici à la fin de l’année, période pendant laquelle les deux produits seront au catalogue. N’hésitez pas à nous dire en commentaire si vous pensez que les deux produits se marchent sur les pieds ou non.

articles.title: Cómo Spotify, YouTube, Apple Music y más apps te muestran que una canción fue hecha con IA
articles.text:
El auge de la música generada por inteligencia artificial está redefiniendo el panorama de las plataformas de streaming. Bandcamp, Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube y más apps han tomado caminos diversos frente a este fenómeno, estableciendo políticas y etiquetas que varían desde la prohibición total hasta la integración con advertencias visibles para el usuario.
Cómo saber que la música que escuchas fue hecha con IA
- Spotify
Spotify aborda la música creada con IA con una estrategia de transparencia y control. A partir de abril de 2026, los creadores pueden especificar en los créditos el uso de IA, detallando si se utilizó solo en una parte, como un riff de guitarra, o en toda la producción.
PUBLICIDAD
Para fortalecer la autenticidad, el servicio introdujo insignias de verificación para creadores humanos y el programa Artist Profile Protection, que permite a los artistas bloquear sus perfiles ante cargas aleatorias no autorizadas.
El paso más destacado llegó en agosto, con la creación de la etiqueta “AI Persona”. Esta marca se aplicará a artistas generados por IA y, a partir de septiembre, la música bajo esta etiqueta quedará excluida de las recomendaciones personalizadas.
PUBLICIDAD
- Apple Music
Apple Music ha optado por visibilizar la música de IA a través de etiquetas. El sistema Made With AI, anunciado en agosto y previsto para finales de 2026, identificará cualquier canción catalogada por proveedores como “generada materialmente con IA”.
La empresa exige desde marzo que los distribuidores revelen el uso de IA en cualquier etapa creativa, desde ilustraciones hasta composiciones y videos. La detección se basa en la divulgación voluntaria, aunque Apple Music utiliza herramientas internas para monitorear el crecimiento de este contenido.
PUBLICIDAD
- YouTube
En YouTube, cada persona que sube contenido generado por IA —incluida la música— debe declarar su uso. La plataforma añade una etiqueta para asegurar la transparencia. No existen, hasta el momento, otras políticas específicas sobre música de IA. Además, Google, empresa matriz de YouTube, continúa desarrollando su propio modelo de creación musical con IA, conocido como Lyria 3, tras la adquisición de ProducerAI.
- SoundCloud
SoundCloud establece límites claros: prohíbe música generada por IA que imite o clone voces de artistas humanos. Todo contenido manipulado por IA debe cumplir los mismos requisitos que las producciones convencionales. SoundCloud también ha declarado que no utiliza música para entrenar modelos de IA generativa y que no lo hará sin consentimiento expreso.
PUBLICIDAD
- Amazon Music
Amazon Music implementa sistemas contra la suplantación, el engaño y el spam, problemas frecuentes en cargas de música generada por IA. Sin embargo, no existen reglas específicas para este tipo de contenido más allá de estas medidas generales. Amazon ha señalado que la comunidad musical está en pleno debate sobre los estándares de etiquetado y que la empresa seguirá explorando formas de informar a los usuarios mientras avanza la discusión.
- Tidal
En junio, Tidal anunció una de las posturas más estrictas de la industria: no monetizará contenido generado por IA y hará responsables a los distribuidores de identificarlo antes de subirlo. La propia plataforma también intentará detectar y etiquetar música de IA, comenzando con la generada en su totalidad y extendiéndose posteriormente a la “sustancialmente generada por IA” conforme la tecnología evolucione.
PUBLICIDAD
- Qobuz
Qobuz se posiciona con una política de “curaduría 100% humana” en sus playlists, artículos y reseñas. La plataforma garantiza que su página Discover filtrará las pistas generadas por IA. Además, identifica transmisiones fraudulentas y las excluye de los fondos de regalías.
Desde enero de 2026, Qobuz incluye cláusulas contractuales que prohíben la entrega de música creada íntegramente por IA y ofrece campos especiales para que artistas y sellos reporten este tipo de contenido.
PUBLICIDAD
- Deezer
Deezer ha sido uno de los servicios más activos y vocales respecto a la música de IA. Desde enero de 2025, utiliza un detector interno para identificar canciones totalmente generadas por IA, llegando a reportar que más del 50% de las cargas diarias, en su punto máximo, provenían de esta tecnología en junio de 2026.
Deezer etiqueta las canciones generadas por IA y las excluye de las recomendaciones algorítmicas o editoriales. Desde julio, elimina pistas de IA sospechosas de fraude de streaming o que no hayan sido reproducidas durante seis meses o más. Según datos internos, hasta el 85% de los streams de canciones generadas completamente por IA eran fraudulentos.
PUBLICIDAD
- Bandcamp
En enero de 2026, Bandcamp marcó un precedente al prohibir toda canción generada por IA, ya sea completamente o en una parte sustancial del proceso creativo. Esta medida fue adoptada poco después de que iHeartRadio anunciara una política similar contra la reproducción de música con vocalistas sintéticos en sus estaciones nacionales. La app también prohíbe el uso de herramientas de IA para suplantar a otros artistas o estilos musicales.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: 'One of the best TVs I've tested in 2026': I review the Sony Bravia 7 II and it shows what RGB LED is capable of — but I'd still pick an OLED
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Sony Bravia 7 II is one of the strongest examples of the new RGB TV group I've tested to date, showcasing great picture quality and gaming performance at an OLED-rivaling price. While its sound could be better, and it has some of the picture issues that come with mini-LED — backlight blooming, weaker-than-OLED viewing angles — it's still a solid TV that shows RGB can give OLED a run for its money.
Pros
- +Great overall picture quality
- +Good gaming performance
- +An evolution of standard mini-LED
Cons
- -Reflective screen
- -Average viewing angles
- -Only two HDMI 2.1 ports
Why you can trust TechRadar
The Sony Bravia 7 II serves as the more affordable model in Sony’s RGB LED 2026 lineup, and while it may not deliver the OLED-rivaling performance RGB has been touted to offer, it’s probably one of the best examples I’ve seen of the new RGB tech in action. It won’t beat the very best TVs I’ve tested this year, but it’s certainly a great TV.
The Bravia 7 II’s picture quality is great overall. It demonstrates excellent backlight control that delivers OLED-level blacks when viewed straight on, with minimal signs of blooming. It also delivers spectacular colors that rival the best OLED TVs, as well as refined, realistic detail and textures that bring pictures to life. It also delivers excellent motion handling for fast-paced action on screen. While not perfect, due to its reflective screen and signs of backlight blooming and faded contrast when viewed off-center, the Bravia 7 II’s picture is still very good.
Sony’s TVs are often among the strongest for built-in sound, but while the Bravia 7 II shows promise, its built-in sound wasn’t quite as good as I hoped. Getting the settings right is key (check out the sound quality section for more info), and once set up, it does deliver a clear, detailed, and accurate sound profile with decent bass. Yet, the sound felt too contained for my liking. I’d recommend one of the best soundbars here if you’re a regular movie viewer.
Gaming is well supported on the Bravia 7 II, with 4K 120Hz, VRR, ALLM and Dolby Vision all featured. The Bravia 7 II even produced a 10.4ms input lag time; one of the stronger times I’ve seen from a Sony TV. This translates well into real-life gaming, as I found performance smooth and responsive. While it has just two HDMI 2.1 ports and its picture can get muddy during fast-paced sequences, the Bravia 7 II still gives the best gaming TVs a run for their money.
Using Google TV as its smart TV platform, the Bravia 7 II has a good number of picture and audio settings, with fairly easy-to-navigate menus. Performance is strong overall, with only the occasional stutter, and while the large banner ads on the home menu can be distracting, Google TV is a decent smart TV platform.
The Bravia 7 II is solid value for money. While it is a premium-priced ‘mid-range’ TV, it delivers very good performance with a strong feature list and even goes toe-to-toe with rival OLEDs like the LG C6. The 65-inch launched at $2,599 / £2,299 / AU$3,299, with prices already dropping to $1,799 / £1,899 / AU$3,295. The Bravia 7 II may still be pricey, but it’s mostly in line with other RGB TVs and OLEDs for what it offers.
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Prices & release dates

- 55-inch price: $2,099 / £1,999 / AU$2,499
- 65-inch price: $2,599 / £2,299 / AU$3,299
- 75-inch price: $3,099 / £2,999 / AU$4,499
- 85-inch price: $3,999 / £3,999 / AU$5,999
The Bravia 7 II is the more affordable model in Sony’s True RGB TV lineup, sitting below the flagship Sony Bravia 9 II. The 65-inch model I tested for my review launched at $2,599 / £2,299 / AU$3,299, putting it at a similar launch price to the LG C6 OLED.

Since its release, the Bravia 7 II has been on sale several times, with the same 65-inch model I tested dropping to $1,799 in the US and £1,999 in the UK. Prices remain unchanged in Australia at the time of writing.

Sony Bravia 7 II review: Features
- RGB mini-LED panel
- XR Processor
- Perfect for PS5 features
The Bravia 7 II is one of Sony’s True RGB TVs and features an RGB mini-LED backlight. This introduces red, green and blue LEDs instead of the normal white you’ll find in a standard LED/mini-LED panel for greater color volume and (generally) higher brightness. Along with the RGB backlight, there are numerous named RGB features, including RGB Backlight Master Drive Pro and RGB Triluminous Max
The Bravia 7 II is equipped with Sony’s own XR Processor, which supports picture features such as XR Clear Image (for better motion clarity), XR Motion Clarity (for smoother motion) and XR Contrast Booster (for enhanced contrast).
Dolby Vision HDR is supported but not HDR10+ (which isn’t unusual for Sony). There's also support for IMAX Enhanced content.
The Bravia 7 II supports an X-Wide Angle Pro feature for better viewing angles, something RGB TVs from most brands say is one of the advantages of the new technology, as standard mini-LED, when viewed from an angle, can often result in backlight blooming.
As for audio, the 65-, 75- and 85-inch models have a 40W speaker system consisting of two full-range speakers and two subwoofers. The 50- and 55-inch models use two full-range speakers and two tweeters. The Bravia 7 II supports AI Voice upscaling and room calibration audio features, and both Dolby Atmos and DTS:X (as well as DTS-HD) audio formats.
For gaming, the Bravia 7 II has two HDMI 2.1 ports that support 4K 120Hz, ALLM and VRR gaming. The other two ports are standard HDMI 2.0. There are also Perfect for PS5 features, including Auto HDR Tone Mapping, Auto Genre Picture Mode (where the TV will automatically switch to game picture mode when a PS5 is detected), and support for the PS Remote Play app, where you can control your PS5, PS5 Pro or PS4 from another location via the TV.
The Bravia 7 II uses Google TV as its smart TV platform and supports the usual streaming apps such as Netflix and Prime Video, as well as Sony’s own Bravia Pictures Core streaming service. In the UK, there is support for BBC iPlayer, ITVX, Channel 4 and Channel 5 streaming apps. In the US, the Bravia 7 II features an ATSC 3.0 tuner.
- Features score: 4.5/5
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Picture quality
- Brilliant color reproduction
- Excellent contrast
- Blooming when viewed off-center
Starting with brightness measurements, the 65-inch Bravia 7 II registered 1,114 nits peak HDR brightness in its Professional picture mode (its equivalent to Filmmaker), 1,295 nits in Standard mode, and 1,163 nits in Cinema mode. This makes it one of the dimmer RGB TVs I’ve tested out of the box, with the Hisense UR8 hitting 2,097 nits and the Samsung R95H hitting 1,977 nits, both in HDR Filmmaker Mode.
As for HDR fullscreen brightness, the Bravia 7 II registered 829 nits in Professional mode, a solid number that beats both the UR8, which hit 771 nits, and the R95H, which hit 612 nits: again, both in Filmmaker Mode.
The Bravia 7 II also registered promising peak SDR brightness in Standard mode, hitting 608 nits, and in Cinema mode, hitting 663 nits, making it a good TV for standard daytime and broadcast TV and other non-HDR sources.
One of the first things I noted about the Bravia 7 II while testing it in our lab is that it has a reflective screen. Any dark scenes viewed in bright lighting showed mirror-like reflections on the screen, especially when there was a lot of black. If you’re watching a darker movie or TV show, it’s definitely worth watching in ambient conditions.
Moving to 4K, HDR content, the Bravia showcases excellent color reproduction: some of the best I’ve seen on an RGB TV so far. Watching The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, colors really pop on-screen with superb vibrancy. As the Lumas all gather in the room for story time, the Lumas themselves are vibrant, showing off the Bravia 7 II’s fantastic color volume. Other bright colors throughout the movie, such as the green of Yoshi’s skin, are bold and rich, too.
In a real-world movie, namely Speed Racer, the Bravia 7 II renders the gaudy interior of the Racer home and their outfits with real accuracy and some impressive clarity. The purple of Royalton Industries is another highlight, where the Bravia 7 II shows excellent highlights and great color luminance.
It’s not surprising the Bravia 7 II delivered brilliant colors as it scored highly in the HDR color gamut coverage tests. It registered 87.7% of the BT.2020 color space and 99.2% of the UHDA-P3 color space: both excellent results that are up there with QD-OLED TVs. While other RGB TVs I’ve tested have broken the scale of the UHDA-P3 coverage, with both the Hisense UR8 and Samsung R95H hitting over 145%, this didn’t stop the Bravia 7 II colors from looking fantastic. In fact, in my Bravia 7 II vs R95H comparison, I often preferred the Bravia 7 II’s color profile. It even gave the C6 a run for its money in my LG C6 vs Bravia 7 II comparison.
The Bravia 7 II’s contrast is strong. In The Batman, the dark walls and floors of the Batcave balance well with the bright tones from the overhead lights and monitors Bruce uses when reviewing video footage. There’s also great shadow detail, where textures such as the back wall of a subway platform Batman stands on are legible while still maintaining rich dark tones.
In Dark City, blacks are deep and inky, and again there’s powerful contrast at work. I did notice some occasional black crush in some scenes. When John is talking to the hotel clerk, the texture of his curly hair isn’t as clear, but black tones are still rich. In my Bravia 7 II vs Samsung R95H comparison, the R95H proved to have better black detail in this scene.
The Bravia 7 II showed superb detail and crisp textures throughout my testing. In footage of a snow-covered deer from the Spears & Munsil UHD Benchmark 4K Blu-ray, the deer has a near-3D-like look, showing some nice depth that really made the image come to life. This is true in other reference scenes I used too, such as how people look in Speed Racer. Skin looks lifelike, and other textures, like the detail of the Mach 5 car, were delivered with gorgeous clarity.
It also demonstrates excellent motion handling, even with motion settings turned off. As cars glided around the track in the opening race of Speed Racer, there were very minimal signs of judder or blur. The Bravia 7 even effectively handled the commentators moving across the screen, something I’ve seen produce serious judder on other TVs.
While I did find that viewing angles of the Bravia 7 II were better than a standard mini-LED, I noted that when viewed from an extreme angle, some backlight blooming was visible, especially in dark scenes. As white text appears against a black background, there's a halo effect around the writing. This is an area where OLED, which RGB aims to rival, is still superior, as OLED has self-dimming pixels for better control. However, the Bravia 7 II did mostly deliver very good backlight control when viewed head-on.
- Picture quality score: 4.5/5
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Sound quality
- Good dynamics and detail
- Effective Acoustic Room Calibration
- Sound can still feel contained to screen
The 65-inch Bravia 7 II has a 40W speaker system, consisting of two full-range speakers and two subwoofers. Rather than the conventional sound modes of other TVs, it focuses on a much more manual approach, with an equalizer and processing settings for users to experiment with.
During the opening race of Speed Racer, the Bravia 7 II delivered accurate sound with clear dynamics. As cars swerved around the track, the sound was accurately mapped to the picture on screen. In one section, as Speed grinds his car on a rail, the subtle grinding noise was audible amongst the chaos of the race. There was some solid, punchy bass capturing the sound of the engines, but I couldn’t help but feel it lacked the ‘oomph’ I’ve come to expect from Sony’s TVs.
Activating Acoustic Room Calibration added some much-needed edge to the sound. The soundstage widened, creating a more immersive sound, and bass was heftier, rendering the roar of the engines more accurately. Voices were clear with and without the calibration, but they were clearer with the calibration active. Atmos effects such as cars flying overhead as they cleared the track’s jumps were also more audible.
Still, the sound could be harsh at times, especially when in the ‘compressed’ dynamic range. I opted for ‘standard’ for a quieter, warmer sound profile. The sound again felt artificial at times, and still felt contained to the rear of the TV. While the overall sound is decent, it won’t beat a good soundbar.
- Sound quality score: 4/5
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Design
- ‘Invisible’ stand
- Hefty build
- Bulkier than rivals
The Bravia 7 II has a central pedestal stand. Made of tough, sturdy metal, the Bravia 7 II feels secure on a tabletop stand, and against the right background (I use a dark-wood stand), the stand can blend in to create a more ‘floating’ look.
The Bravia 7 II itself is on the weightier side, mainly due to its bulkier frame. Compared to many other TVs in today’s market, the Bravia 7 II is much deeper and thicker, probably to handle its built-in speakers. The TV's bezel is trim, allowing plenty of room for the pictures on screen.
There are two remotes included with the Bravia 7 II (one mainly for UK users, as it has numbered buttons), but the main one is the Bravia Voice Remote. The button layout is functional and easy enough to understand, but it feels on the cheap side, being made of light plastic. For a TV at this price, I’d have liked a more premium remote.
- Design score: 4/5
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Smart TV & menus
- Google TV
- Good number of settings
- Ads and performance can frustrate
Like most Sony TVs, the Bravia 7 II uses Google TV as its smart TV platform. Once logged in with your Google account, there will be recommendations from various apps based on your viewing history, which is useful for finding new content. However, the home page is beset with large banner ads that sometimes fill half the screen, which can be very distracting. Google TV supports all major streaming apps, including UK-based platforms such as BBC iPlayer and ITVX.
In terms of settings, the Bravia 7 II has plenty of picture settings and modes for users to get stuck into. There are tons of ways to customize picture settings, with AI-based tools and more traditional brightness, color, contrast and motion settings. The aforementioned sound settings (in the Sound Quality section) also allow for some freedom, but can be daunting for those looking for easy set-up.
I did find that while navigating through some apps and menus, the Bravia 7 II’s performance could stutter at times. This was also true when using the UB-820 4K Blu-ray player, with some stutters here and there. Performance for the most part was solid; just not as slick as on LG’s TVs, say.
- Smart TV & menus score: 4/5
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Gaming
- 10.4ms input lag time
- 4K 120Hz and VRR supported
- Only two HDMI 2.1 ports
The Bravia 7 II supports 4K 120Hz, VRR, Dolby Vision gaming and ALLM, featured on two HDMI 2.1 ports. Using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester, I measured the Bravia 7 II’s input lag at 10.4ms at 4K 60Hz, which is a big improvement over other Sony TVs we’ve tested at TechRadar, such as the Bravia 8 II OLED, which clocked in at 16.3ms (4K 60Hz). The Bravia 7 II also registered 5.7ms at 1080p 120Hz: a solid time compared to other TVs I’ve tested this year.
These strong input lag times translate to actual gaming. Playing Battlefield V on Xbox Series X, the Bravia 7 II demonstrated responsive performance, which felt smooth even during chaotic battle sequences with a lot of free-flowing movement. Locking onto targets felt snappy with almost no signs of judder.
The Bravia 7 II’s picture quality while gaming was strong for the most part, showing excellent detail with 3D-like textures, as well as bold brightness, rich contrast and punchy colors. I did notice that during faster-paced moments, a dirt screen effect could occur, where textures became a bit muddied, but this didn’t happen all the time.
- Gaming score: 4.5/5
Sony Bravia 7 II review: Value
- Solid value
- Very good performance and features
- Similar price bracket to LG OLED C6
The Bravia 7 II is a mid-range model, and while its 65-inch model, which currently costs $1,799 / £1,899 / AU$3,295, is a premium price tag for this price bracket, it performs well for the money, giving both the LG C6 and Samsung R95H (Samsung’s flagship RGB TV) a run for their money when I tested them side-by-side: and it’s cheaper than both.
The Bravia 7 II’s closest OLED competitor is the LG C6, which costs $1,799 / £2,099 / AU$3,295 for a 65-inch, meaning it’s the same price in both the US and Australia. While the Bravia 7 II doesn’t quite top the C6 in terms of value for money, as it's missing some features, like four HDMI 2.1 ports, which the C6 has, the Bravia 7 II is good overall value for money in the new RGB world.
- Value score: 4/5
Should I buy the Sony Bravia 7 II?
| Sony Bravia 7 II |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Good gaming features, smart features and performance | 4.5/5 | 
| Picture quality | Stunning colors, detail and great backlight control overall, but blooming appears when viewed off-center. Its screen is quite reflective too. | 4.5/5 | 
| Sound quality | Solid sound quality overall when set up correctly, with good detail and accuracy. Sound does feel contained to the screen and can be harsh at times. | 4/5 | 
| Design | Solid overall build quality, but is on the denser, deeper side in terms of scale. | 4.5/5 | 
| Smart TV and menus | Google TV has good app access and content recommendations, but banner ads are distracting. Great picture and sound settings. | 4/5 | 
| Gaming | Great gaming performance with low input-lag times. Solid picture, but some dirty screen effect can happen. Only two HDMI 2.1 ports could be a problem for some gamers. | 5/5 | 
| Value | Consistent price with other RGB TVs and good performance and features for the money. LG C6 is available for the same price, however. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You want great overall picture quality
The Bravia 7 II shows what RGB TVs can be capable of, with excellent color reproduction, strong contrast and black tones and better-than-mini-LED backlight control. 
You want a gaming RGB TV
With 4K 120Hz, Dolby Vision gaming, VRR and ALLM supported, plus a 10.4ms input lag time, the Bravia 7 II is a strong gaming TV. 
You want to see what RGB LED can do
While some RGB TVs I've tested so far haven't quite lived up to the hype, the Bravia 7 II shows what the new tech is capable of at a more 'affordable' price point. 
Don't buy it if...
You'll be watching from an angle
While off-center viewing is still decent, backlight blooming and faded contrast can appear when watching the Bravia 7 II from an angle. 
You have a very bright room
The Bravia 7 II does have a reflective screen, which can make watching darker scenes difficult in brighter viewing conditions. 
You need multiple HDMI 2.1 ports for gaming
The Bravia 7 II only has two HDMI 2.1 ports (one of which is eARC), so if you have multiple consoles and a soundbar, you'll struggle for space. 
Also Consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Sony Bravia 7 II | LG C6 | Samsung R95H | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Price (65-inch) | $2,599 / £2,299 / AU$3,299 | $2,699 / £2,599 / AU$3,995 | $2,999 / £3,099 / AU$4,999 | 
| Screen type | RGB LED | OLED | Micro RGB | 
| Refresh rate | 120Hz | 165Hz | 165Hz | 
| HDR support | Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG | HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | 
| Smart TV | Google TV | webOS 26 | Samsung Vision AI (Tizen) | 
| HDMI ports | 4 (2 x HDMI 2.1) | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 
LG C6
The main OLED rival of the Bravia 7 II, the LG C6 is one of 2026's best TVs, delivering excellent picture quality and performance. While the C6 offers better contrast, colors, and black tones, along with a full suite of gaming features, the Bravia 7 II went toe-to-toe with the C6 when I tested them side-by-side. They're both in a similar price bracket, so it comes down to panel tech preference. 
Read our full LG C6 review
Samsung R95H
Samsung's flagship Micro RGB TV is brighter than the Bravia 7 II and has more gaming features, while also delivering the same strong contrast and backlight performance. In my head-to-head test of the two, the Bravia 7 II's colors and detail were stronger overall, however. The Bravia 7 II is also significantly cheaper. 
Read our Bravia 7 II vs R95H comparison
Hisense UR8
Hisense's affordable RGB mini-LED, the UR8, delivers good picture quality and features at a very competitive price in the US and Australia. While it delivers similar contrast and backlight control to the Bravia 7 II, the latter delivers stronger colors and detail that give it better picture quality. 
Read our Hisense UR8 review
How I tested the Sony Bravia 7 II
- Tested over several weeks in our testing lab
- Tested in both light and dark conditions
- Measurements taken using Portrait Displays' Calman Color Calibration software
Before conducting my full testing of the Sony Bravia 7 II, I first did some casual viewing to establish its best picture modes, opting for Professional mode in darker conditions and Cinema mode for brighter conditions and brighter movies.
I next moved on to critical viewing, using reference scenes from 4K Blu-ray to test color, contrast, detail, motion, upscaling and backlight performance. I also used SDR sources such as DVD, broadcast TV, and lower-resolution streaming.
I also used reference scenes from movies such as Speed Racer and The Batman to test the Bravia 7 II's built-in speakers.
Once these subjective tests were complete, I took testing measurements using Portrait Displays Calman Color Calibration software and specialized equipment, including a Murideo Six G 8K Metal test pattern generator and a Klein 10-A colorimeter, which was profiled with a Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer.
The first measurements I took were of the Bravia 7 II's brightness. Using 1-100% white window patterns, in both HDR and SDR, I focused primarily on the 10% (for peak brightness) and 100% (for full-screen brightness) window patterns, which are featured in the graphs above.
Next, I measured its HDR color gamut coverage, using both the UHDA-P3 and BT.2020 color spaces.
I also measured its grayscale and color accuracy in SDR using Delta-E values (the margin of error between the test pattern signal and what the screen shows) to determine its accuracy, hoping for a score below 3.
Finally, I measured its input lag using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester, measuring both 4K 60Hz and 1080p 120Hz in milliseconds.

articles.title: As Tim Cook steps down, India stands at the heart of Apple’s next chapter
articles.text:
As Tim Cook steps down, India stands at the heart of Apple’s next chapter
Tim Cook, once Steve Jobs’ operations man who made Apple’s ‘trains run on time’, turned India from a market of promise into a key centre for sales and production. His successor must now take that two-sided bet deeper.
The night before Tim Cook arrived in Hyderabad in May 2016, I was told to get there and try to get him on camera. While most TV news crews waited at Apple’s office, my cameraman and I took a chance on the VIP exit at Hyderabad airport. Cook emerged with his entourage, and I managed to ask him two questions as we walked towards his car. The exchange lasted barely 30 seconds, but it made our business news channel the first to get a sound bite from Cook that morning.
The visit itself had greater significance. Apple opened its maps development centre in Hyderabad and announced an iOS app design and development accelerator in Bengaluru, giving its long-standing India ambitions a more tangible shape. A decade later, as Cook steps down as Apple CEO on August 31 after 15 years at the helm, India occupies a very different place in the company’s plans.
Apple’s annual sales in India crossed $10 billion for the first time in the year ended March 2026, according to Bloomberg. Its physical retail network has expanded beyond the first stores it opened in Mumbai and Delhi in 2023. India also assembled about 55 million iPhones in 2025, or roughly a quarter of Apple’s global production. The numbers capture the evolution of Cook’s India bet.
He came to see the country as two opportunities at once: a growing market for Apple products and an alternative production base as the company sought to reduce its dependence on China. The two bets did not mature at the same pace, and neither is complete. Apple remains a premium player in a price-sensitive smartphone market. India, meanwhile, is still some distance from matching the depth and efficiency of China’s electronics supply chain. But Cook leaves behind a company for which India is no longer a market that is always about to arrive. It is now central to how Apple sells and where it makes its most important product.
The long wait for Indian consumers
Cook’s optimism about India long preceded Apple’s commercial breakthrough in the country. The opportunity appeared obvious. India had a large, young population, rising incomes, and hundreds of millions of smartphone users. Yet converting those advantages into iPhone sales proved difficult.
Import duties made Apple’s products more expensive. Rules governing foreign-owned retail complicated its plans to open stores. The company was also competing in a market where the largest volumes came from devices priced far below the iPhone.
Apple did not chase India’s mass market. It waited for more Indian consumers to move up to the iPhone. The company began assembling iPhones locally in 2017, initially using Wistron to produce older models in Bengaluru. Local assembly helped reduce some of the disadvantages associated with importing finished devices.
Apple opened its online store in India in 2020, giving it a direct relationship with customers. In April 2023, Cook returned to India to open the company’s first physical stores in Mumbai and Delhi. The retail network has since expanded to other cities. The stores were about more than adding sales points. They gave Apple greater control over how its products were presented and allowed it to offer financing, trade-ins, technical support and the wider Apple experience directly to customers.
At the same time, India’s smartphone market was changing. More consumers were willing to pay for premium devices. No-cost instalments, exchange programmes and lower-priced older-generation iPhones made the brand accessible to a wider group without requiring Apple to abandon its premium positioning. Apple’s India revenue was close to $6 billion in the year ended March 2023, up from $4.1 billion a year earlier. Three years later, annual sales reportedly crossed $10 billion.
In one of his last earnings calls as CEO, Tim Cook was ‘over the moon’ on India growth, counting the country among Apple’s strongest-performing markets. That growth matters because Apple has achieved it without competing seriously in the segments that generate most of India’s smartphone volumes. The company has instead benefited from the expansion of the premium category, a segment it has helped shape. But the most consequential part of Cook’s legacy may lie on the production side.
From selling iPhones to making them
Long before he succeeded Steve Jobs as CEO, Cook was the operator who made Apple’s ‘trains run on time’. He streamlined inventory, suppliers and manufacturing, building a supply chain capable of producing complex devices at enormous scale and healthy margins. That machine also left Apple heavily dependent on China. The pandemic, disruptions at major factories, rising tensions between Washington and Beijing, and the threat of tariffs exposed the risks of that concentration. Apple needed additional production centres, even if replacing China entirely was neither practical nor desirable.
India emerged as Apple’s most important alternative base for iPhone production. What began in 2017 with the assembly of older devices expanded to include Apple’s latest and premium models. Foxconn increased its manufacturing footprint, while Tata Electronics emerged as a major Indian partner after taking over Wistron’s local operations and acquiring a controlling stake in Pegatron’s India business.
Apple assembled about 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53% increase from the previous year, according to Bloomberg. That represented roughly 25% of its estimated global iPhone output. India now supplies a growing share of the iPhones sold in Apple’s largest consumer market, the US. In 2025, Cook said a majority of the iPhones sold in the US during the June quarter would have India as their country of origin. Vietnam, meanwhile, would supply most of the iPads, Macs, Apple Watches and AirPods sold in the US. This is the real significance of the India manufacturing story. India is not merely producing iPhones for Indian consumers. It is becoming an export base for Apple’s global operations.
iPhone exports from India crossed an estimated Rs 2 lakh crore in FY26, according to reports based on vendor submissions and government trade data. Apple’s vendors now account for a substantial share of the country’s smartphone exports, making the company one of the most visible beneficiaries of India’s production-linked incentive programme for electronics manufacturing.
For the Indian government, Apple has become evidence that global electronics supply chains can be persuaded to move to the country. For Apple, India offers scale, policy support and an alternative to concentrating so much production in China. It has also given the company greater flexibility at a time when tariffs and geopolitics increasingly influence where products are manufactured.
Assembly is only the first step
The rapid growth in iPhone production can, however, make Apple’s India presence appear deeper than it is. India assembles a growing number of iPhones, but many of the high-value components inside them continue to come from overseas. China retains a network of suppliers, engineers, tooling companies, logistics providers and skilled workers built over several decades.
That ecosystem allows Apple to move from product design to mass production with a speed and flexibility that India cannot yet match. The distinction matters. Producing a larger number of finished iPhones does not automatically mean India is capturing a proportionate share of their value. The next stage will depend on whether Apple and its partners can localise more components, improve manufacturing yields, develop specialised skills and bring a wider group of suppliers into the country. India must also provide stable policies, efficient ports, reliable infrastructure and the large pools of trained workers needed to support factories operating at Apple’s scale. The consumer opportunity has similar limits.
India may have crossed $10 billion in annual sales for Apple, but the iPhone remains unaffordable for most smartphone buyers. Apple must find ways to reach more consumers without weakening the premium positioning that supports its margins and brand. That is the unfinished part of Cook’s India bet. It is also the job Ternus inherits.
What John Ternus must do next
Cook is giving up the CEO role, but not leaving Apple. From September 1, he will become executive chairman and continue to assist the company, including in its engagement with policymakers. John Ternus, Apple’s longtime hardware engineering chief, takes over as CEO at a time when the company faces questions about artificial intelligence, its next major product category and the resilience of its supply chain. India will be central to how Ternus tackles at least one of them: Apple’s dependence on China.
Ternus must build on the consumer momentum by expanding retail, strengthening the developer ecosystem and selling more services alongside devices. On the manufacturing side, the task is to move India beyond final assembly and make it a larger source of components, engineering expertise and supplier capacity. More Indian customers give Apple a reason to invest here. A deeper local supply chain, in turn, makes India more important to Apple globally. When I caught Cook outside Hyderabad airport in 2016, Apple’s India ambitions still rested largely on what it planned to do next. A decade later, the factories, stores and sales numbers have made that bet far more concrete.
Cook established Apple’s two-sided India bet. Ternus must now take it deeper.
