articles.title: At least three exhibitors got robbed at Gamescom 2026 — laptops and handhelds with unfinished game builds stolen from locked cabinets
articles.text:
At least three exhibitors got robbed at Gamescom 2026 — laptops and handhelds with unfinished game builds stolen from locked cabinets
The incident has got a solo indie developer in tears.
Several developers and game publishers at Gamescom 2026 in Cologne, Germany, have reported equipment theft at the exhibition. According to Video Games Chronicle (VGC), Mimic developer Ryan Laley, game publisher iam8bit, and Tessera Studios were all hit during the week.
Laley reportedly lost all his laptops from his booth, while iam8bit said in its X post that it’s missing two laptops as well. Meanwhile, Tessera Studios had two laptops and a Steam Deck taken from its cabinet. Laley’s and iam8bit’s booths are located together in Hall 4.1, next to the west entrance gate, meaning they’re both easy targets for thieves looking for a quick score. However, Tessera Studios is in Hall 10.2, putting it quite far from the other two targets.
The cost of the stolen equipment will certainly be a huge setback for these developers and publishers, especially for smaller indie creators. However, the bigger loss would be the data on the machines, which often includes unreleased builds of the games they’re demoing at the expo. While they may have backup copies of their work stored in some of the best external SSDs, the fact that a copy of the games they’re working on is out in the wild and could potentially be leaked would chill the blood of any developer and could be “heartbreaking” for the team working on it.
“Today at gamescom we arrived at our station in the business area hall to discover that our two laptops had been stolen overnight, despite the presence of Koelnmesse security,” iam8bit said in their X post. “These were machines we were using to demo iam8bit Presents titles Petal Runner and Escape Academy 2 to media and content creators during the show. On top of obviously disrupting our very busy appointment schedule, this theft has potentially put unfinished builds of these games at risk of being leaked.”
“On Wednesday, we arrived at our booth in the Indie Area to find our cabinet forced open. Two laptops and a Steam Deck were gone,” Tessera Studios posted on X. “The devices contained not only our Gamescom demo, but also personal, company, and critical information.”
Gamescom organizers responded to the issues, saying that although they have arranged for uniformed guards to provide general security, individual booth security must be booked separately. They’ve also advised exhibitors to have insurance against theft, and said these warnings are noted in the terms and conditions for participants, as well as in the event’s technical guidelines.
“All cases have been reported to us and to the police, and investigations are already underway,” the organizers’ statement read. They also said that security is one of their priorities at the event, but also added, “At an event of this size, however, there will always be individuals attempting to take advantage of the situation.”
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

articles.title: Musk's faster path to more gas turbines comes with pollution problem | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Elon Musk says he’s found a way to solve one of AI’s biggest bottlenecks by making a hard-to-manufacture turbine part himself.
On Saturday, Musk confirmed what a secret foundry SpaceX has been building in Bastrop, Texas, is for — an apparent response to a story that was already closing in on the details. Earlier in the day, The Information published a report citing job listings that explicitly mention a “blades and vanes foundry,” plus findings from Corey Trinetti, a due diligence specialist who authors detailed reviews of AI infrastructure sites in his newsletter and who’d reported that SpaceX had bought roughly 830 acres near its existing Starlink factory in Bastrop between March and June.
“SpaceX and Tesla are each building 100GW/year of solar production capacity as fast as possible,” Musk wrote on X on Saturday, “but natural gas will still be needed to supplement and bootstrap solar for several years. The limiting factor for nat gas turbine production is casting the blades & vanes. By doing in-house casting at SpaceX, we can accelerate nat gas turbines coming online by up to 18 months, which is a profound game-changer.”
The “why” of all this goes back to one of the biggest challenges facing the AI industry right now. GPU shortages are still an issue — Nvidia’s newest Blackwell chips are still running lead times of several months, for example — but a second constraint has emerged alongside it, which is the physical power grid. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity use will roughly double by 2030, and gas turbine maker GE Vernova says it’s essentially sold out of production capacity through 2030 due largely to AI infrastructure demand.
That shortage is why building private gas-fired plants next to data centers, instead of waiting on the grid, has become a ubiquitous strategy for so-called hyperscalers, including Amazon, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and Microsoft. After years of prioritizing wind and solar, they’re all now betting on natural gas to get data centers online faster.
As for the casting bottleneck specifically, according to The Information, the blades inside a gas turbine’s hottest section run at temperatures around 3,000 to 3,600 degrees Fahrenheit, which is roughly 800 degrees hotter than the melting point of the very metal alloy they’re made from. That’s only possible because of the blades’ internal cooling channels and thermal-barrier coatings, plus the specific way each blade is cast. Just four companies worldwide have mastered the casting process well enough to produce them at industrial scale, and all of them are tapped out right now.
What makes the whole thing especially difficult is that each blade has to be cast as a single, unbroken crystal, grown slowly inside a vacuum furnace, without the microscopic seams that let ordinary cast metal crack under stress. It’s a tricky process even for the smaller blades used in jet engines; the blades in power-plant turbines are considerably larger, which makes producing them at that scale and without defects even harder.
If SpaceX pulls this off — and it’s easier said than done, of course — it would mean a Musk-controlled entity holds a manufacturing capability that every other AI infrastructure builder currently depends on a tiny oligopoly for, giving SpaceXAI an edge that’s difficult for any well-funded but non-manufacturing competitor to copy quickly.
But it would also mean more gas turbines coming on fast, and turbines in the ground are already drawing federal lawsuits and peer-reviewed health research over the pollution they emit.
In Memphis, where SpaceXAI has run gas turbines to power its Colossus data centers since 2024, the NAACP has repeatedly accused the company of operating turbines without the permits or pollution controls required by federal law. The organization’s concern is that turbines like these emit smog-forming compounds and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde, pollutants linked to asthma, respiratory disease, and certain cancers. (The site sits near neighborhoods that already face heavy industrial pollution, and University of Memphis researchers said that in their own admittedly limited analysis, air pollution grew “slightly worse” because of the data center.)
But Memphis just happens to be the most visible case. The same fight is playing out anywhere gas turbines have become the default fix for data center power shortages. In Virginia’s “Data Center Alley,” a study commissioned by the Piedmont Environmental Council used the EPA’s own COBRA health-impact model to assess a single facility’s eight full-time gas turbines. It found their emissions could reach more than 2.5 million people across multiple counties — with the heaviest impact landing on already-marginalized communities — and cause an estimated 3.4 to 6.5 additional premature deaths a year, translating to $53 million to $99 million in annual health-related damages.

articles.title: ¿Tiene 'GTA 6' microtransacciones e IA generativa? Rockstar responde
articles.text:
Tras el reciente vistazo extendido a GTA 6, la expectación de los fanáticos está en niveles altísimos. La cuenta regresiva hacia el lanzamiento del título sigue en marcha sin complicaciones, y Rockstar Games se está abriendo de a poco a entregar más detalles sobre el título. El estudio incluso ha resuelto las dudas sobre dos temas siempre polémicos dentro de la industria: las microtransacciones y el uso de IA generativa.
Según Kinda Funny Games, desde la compañía no anduvieron con rodeos al referirse a ambas cuestiones. El citado medio indicó que tras consultar a Rockstar sobre si GTA 6 permitiría a los usuarios desbloquear nuevos ítems o elementos usando dinero real, la respuesta fue un tajante "no".
En tal sentido, la compañía les comentó que la versión de GTA 6 para un solo jugador no tendrá ningún tipo de monetización. Si bien no se ofrecieron detalles más profundos sobre esta cuestión, la respuesta no sorprende. Rockstar todavía no lo ha confirmado, ni tampoco ha realizado anuncios en tal sentido, pero todo apunta a que eventualmente el nuevo juego tendrá su propio GTA Online.
No olvidemos que el multijugador en línea de GTA V es una máquina de imprimir billetes, pues genera cientos de millones de dólares anuales. Así que es lógico creer que tarde o temprano llegará el componente online de GTA 6 para explorar la monetización que no se ha incluido en la versión single player del juego.
¿Y qué pasa con la IA generativa en GTA 6?
El boom de la IA generativa ha llevado a su adopción en un sinfín de juegos, tanto independientes como de grandes estudios. Esto ha derivado en varias polémicas, especialmente por el plagio de activos generados por artistas reales que fueron replicados por la inteligencia artificial. Pero también por el temor a que se intente reducir la mano de obra real para volcarse a pleno por la citada tecnología.
Si bien Strauss Zelnick, jefe de Take-Two Interactive, se ha mostrado optimista sobre la IA generativa y su capacidad de reducir los costes de producción, también ha sido bastante vocal sobre su exclusión del desarrollo de GTA 6. "En lo que respecta específicamente a GTA 6, la IA generativa no tiene ninguna participación en lo que Rockstar Games está desarrollando. Sus mundos están hechos a mano. Eso es lo que los diferencia. Se construyen desde cero, edificio a edificio, calle a calle, barrio a barrio. No se generan proceduralmente, no deberían. Eso es lo que hace que el entretenimiento sea excelente", dijo el ejecutivo en febrero pasado.
Es por ello que no sorprende que desde Rockstar hayan ratificado en los últimos días que GTA 6 no incluye contenidos creados con IA generativa. Es imposible saber si esto va a cambiar en el futuro, pero al menos para el debut del juego en PS5 y Xbox Series X|S de noviembre no debería haber polémicas en tal sentido.

articles.title: Trust, But Verify
articles.text:
We trust designers to do the best they can, but know they cannot be perfect. That’s why we verify. When AI gets involved, it cannot be trusted.
We have to thank the Russians for the expression, ‘trust but verify’ (doveryai, no proveryai). Suzanne Massie, a scholar of Russian history, taught it to Ronald Reagan while he was president. He then used it to talk about nuclear disarmament discussions with the Soviet Union. Since then, it has been used extensively in many geopolitical contexts, especially those related to security, where you provide the carrot (we trust you), then the stick (no, we don’t).
Long before it became an English proverb, it was being used in practice, especially in the emerging semiconductor industry. Back when I was an undergraduate doing my dissertation, I encountered several forms of it.
I was designing a universal in-circuit emulator and used a pre-production version of the Hilo2 simulator to verify it. Yes, I did find bugs in the simulator, which led to it providing incorrect verification data. Tools are never perfect, and this remains a potential source of problems for every stage of the design, verification, and implementation process. This is probably mild compared to the types of errors we can expect from AI.
Second, I found several errors at the boundaries of specification – a very real problem for most designs even today. In this case I misread a specification, which led to the wrong polarity on an enable signal. If that had been in a real device, I would have blown up most of my drivers. And yes, there were many design errors. I was young, inexperienced, and in a hurry.
Later in my career, I encountered two more types of specification errors. The first of these was an omission in the specification. An undocumented opcode led the processor to violate the hardware/software contract, an error that had serious consequences for every safety-critical design that used that processor.
Another error was discovered where the interrupt subsystem of a processor did not match the specification. It was unclear which was right, but it would have caused problems if you had designed according to the specification.
When using AI, especially in the context of interpreting a specification to create a set of properties, it most certainly cannot be trusted. It is probably not as good as a junior engineer today. Plus, it is being given a totally inadequate specification to start with. But there are real fears about it cheating, as well. In multi-agentic frameworks, trust will be difficult to ascertain without looking at full provenance information — assuming that is provided and hasn’t been tampered with, as well.
We already have several real examples where AI has worked out how to cheat in order to attain a goal. Unless a spec-to-properties tool is forbidden from accessing anything except the specification, it will likely create vacuous properties by peeking at the design, especially if the goal is to increase verification coverage. Even if told it cannot look at anything except the spec, it could ask another agent to do it, or ask another agent to update a specification so it becomes available. There are many ways for AI to cheat, and I don’t think anyone is treating that as a potential problem today.
We not only need to use what AI produces to perform the verification task, as we do today, but we must also verify everything it produces, including its provenance. Doing that requires someone with enough skill to know if they are being conned. Many people already talk about AI being able to produce stuff that looks plausible, but which is nonsense. This is not just about verification. It’s about verification of trust.
As soon as a goal is set, AI has everything it needs to cheat. We are racing ahead without putting in the necessary safeguards. This is happening everywhere AI is deployed, not just in the semiconductor development flow. We are all racing for higher productivity, faster turnaround times, but it will stop, or at least pause, when someone notices that AI has created false trust that leads to failure.
Where are the Asimov (another Russian) laws of robots for AI? Where are the safeguards and rules that all AI is bound by? Nobody has stopped to define them, and that will hurt us all in some manner.
But that is only the beginning of the implications of having AI do this task. Many people have told me that AI will take over the mundane tasks, allowing engineers to be more creative. That is a dream, not reality. It will indirectly create more, but different, mundane tasks, like checking everything AI has done. In an article I wrote this month, several people mentioned that AI will be able to create lots of properties almost instantaneously, but every one of those has to be manually checked. This is instead of a human creating a few high-quality properties that are used in verification.
Maybe senior engineers will spend more time creating better specs and training data on which AI can learn. Then the junior engineers will do the trust-but-verify for the AI-created outputs. In that case, the creative part has been replaced by more mundane tasks. Creation was the fun part. Now they are spending more time in verification. They will spend most of their time checking up on what AI has done.
Will that lead to moral issues within a team? Perhaps, but this is also looking at how to fit AI into the flows we already have. It goes against the notion of allowing the junior engineers to be the ones with the truly creative streak, not bound by the constraints of today’s methods, so long as they understand that they are junior and that means they make mistakes — not on purpose, but because of a lack of maturity and experience.
Run fast, make mistakes, and learn. Engineers do that. Can AI do that? And does it have a moral compass to guide it?

articles.title: Openclaw 2.0 ist da: Das bringt das bislang größte Projekt-Update
articles.text:
Größte Aktualisierung der Projektgeschichte: Diese Neuerungen bringt Openclaw 2.0
Ende 2025 hatte der österreichische Entwickler Peter Steinberger mit seinem quelloffenen KI-Projekt Openclaw für Furore gesorgt. Gedacht als einfache Verbindungsmöglichkeit von Anthropics Claude an den Whatsapp-Messenger erwuchs daraus in kurzer Zeit ein mächtiger KI-Assistent mit riesiger Fangemeinde.
Openclaw: Größtes Update der Projektgeschichte
Jetzt hat Steinberger, der mittlerweile bei OpenAI arbeitet, das bisher größte Openclaw-Update seiner noch jungen Geschichte veröffentlicht. Wie es im Firmenblog heißt, sei Openclaw 2.0 aber eher versehentlich in solche Dimensionen gewachsen. Ursprünglich habe man lediglich die Installation vereinfachen und eine neue Browser-App an den Start bringen wollen.
Daraus entwickelte sich allerdings ein nahezu vollständiger Umbau der Plattform. Betroffen seien davon „Installation, Messaging, Speicher, Skills, Modelle, Automatisierungen, Browser und native Apps, Plugins und Sicherheit“, wie es in der Release-Ankündigung heißt. Außerdem haben die Entwickler:innen eine Reihe von Fehlern behoben.
16.000 Pull Requests von 933 Contributors
Laut Openclaw umfasst das Update mehr als 16.000 Pull Requests von 933 Mitwirkenden, 569 von ihnen waren zum ersten Mal dabei. Die Entwicklung dauerte fast sieben Wochen. Im Vergleich zu früheren Aktualisierungen ein ungewöhnlich langer Zeitraum. In den ersten 230 Tagen hatte Openclaw insgesamt 106 Releases an den Start gebracht.
Zu den sichtbarsten Neuerungen in Openclaw 2.0 gehört die neue Browser-Oberfläche, bei der – ähnlich wie bei ChatGPT oder Gemini – die Konversation in die Mitte rückt. Zur Navigation dient die Seitenleiste. Dateien, Git-Änderungen und der integrierte Browser lassen sich neben dem Chat offenhalten, wie trendingtopics.eu schreibt.
Einfacherer Einstieg in Openclaw 2.0
Darüber hinaus hat Openclaw am Einstieg geschraubt. Bei der Installation durchsucht der KI-Assistent den Computer der Nutzer:innen nach bestehenden ChatGPT- oder Claude-Abos, lokal laufende KI-Modelle sowie API-Keys. Ziel ist es, dass Nutzer:innen schneller bei der ersten Konversation landen und den Rest mithilfe des Assistenten einrichten können.
Interessant ist, dass die Sitzungsverläufe jetzt in einer SQLite-Datenbank abgelegt werden. Das beschleunigt das Laden der Historie. Auch die neue Volltextsuche basiert auf diesem System. Neu ist außerdem, dass Sitzungen das eigene Gerät verlassen und auf gekoppelten Systemen oder in die Cloud wandern können.
Der Kontrolle der Agenten dient eine sogenannte dauerhafte Fortschrittskarte in Openclaw 2.0. Darin sind die Aktivitäten und Änderungen sichtbar. Auch beim Thema Sicherheit, etwa was Passwörter und Berechtigungen bei automatisierten Vorgängen betrifft, hat Openclaw nachgeschärft. Alle Details zum Openclaw-Update sind in den Release Notes nachzulesen.

articles.title: Clinical-Grade Home Light Therapy Devices: Wavelength Accuracy, Dual-Chip Design and Build Quality Explained - Tech Guide
articles.text:
There has been a shift in the use of red and near-infrared light therapy from professional clinics into homes. This shift has led to the design and manufacturing of more sophisticated RLT devices that incorporate multiple wavelengths, have more advanced LED designs, employ efficient optical systems, and offer more detailed performance specifications.
But what does “clinical-grade” actually mean when applied to at-home RLT devices? Since this term is not a universal technical standard, consumers need to look beyond the label and understand specifications like wavelength accuracy, irradiance, treatment dose, coverage, and electrical safety at a deeper level to find out how thoughtfully a device has been designed and engineered.
This article explains these intricacies about RLT devices to help you understand what clinical-grade means for home light therapy devices and how to evaluate these devices in terms of wavelength accuracy, dual-chip design, and build quality.
What Defines a Clinical-Grade Home Light Therapy Device?
The phrase “clinical-grade” does sound reassuring. However, from a consumer’s point of view, it can be difficult to determine what it actually represents because there is no specific requirement or feature that makes any RLT device clinical-grade.
Hence, instead of simply relying on the term clinical-grade, it is important to consider the engineering principles of the device you plan to choose to ensure you achieve the benefits you expect from your RLT sessions.
For example, a well-designed light therapy device should provide consistent and predictable exposure to red and near-infrared light. This feature comes from clearly defined wavelengths, high-quality LEDs and lenses, irradiance at a specified distance, an efficient power supply and cooling system, and robust physical construction. Checking this technical information can help you make informed choices.
In addition, electrical safety and other certifications are other important parameters to consider when choosing an RLT device.
In short, the term “clinical-grade” should be understood as one of the marks of the quality of engineering and intended performance rather than as a guarantee of clinical outcomes.
Why Wavelength Accuracy Matters in Modern Light Therapy Technology
Wavelength is one of the most important features of photobiomodulation technology. The accuracy of wavelengths can play a key role in determining the results you can achieve from your RLT sessions.
Most RLT devices use wavelengths of around 630 to 680 nm in the visible red range and approximately 810 to 850 nm in the near-infrared range. These wavelengths differ in their abilities to penetrate tissue. This is why some manufacturers combine several wavelengths in a single device to help you get benefits associated with a wider spectrum of red and infrared light.
However, not all devices available on the market produce wavelengths they claim in every circumstance. Factors like manufacturing tolerances, operating temperatures, electrical conditions, and the quality of components can influence the actual output of wavelengths. Also, small differences in wavelengths can affect how your device interacts with your biological tissue.
Therefore, it is important to choose an RLT device that supports higher-quality engineering aimed at controlling and testing LED output and is transparent about meaningful technical information. This gives you a better basis for comparison instead of relying on broad claims such as “full spectrum” or “maximum power.”
Dual-Chip LED Design: Improving Output Consistency and Device Performance
A dual-chip configuration basically contains two semiconductor chips capable of producing different wavelengths instead of one light-emitting chip per LED package. This technology allows multiple wavelengths to be incorporated into a relatively compact RLT device. This means a single LED package may be engineered to deliver both red and near-infrared wavelengths. This is expected to broaden the application of red light therapy and enhance the benefits of your sessions.
Reputed manufacturers like BestQool are using dual-chip LED technology in their red light therapy devices to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of their devices.
Beyond Wavelengths: Understanding Irradiance, Dose, and Coverage
Parameters and specifications other than wavelengths, such as irradiance and coverage, influence the efficient functioning of RLT devices.
Irradiance describes how much optical power is delivered to a specific area. It is typically expressed in mW/cm² (milliwatts per square centimeter).
Being aware of what irradiance means for your RLT session is important for choosing the right device. For example, a device may advertise a high irradiance figure. However, that number can offer meaningful results only when measurement conditions like distance and treatment dose are clearly stated.
Distance from the panel can affect the amount of light that actually reaches the area of treatment on your skin or tissue, while the treatment dose depends on the duration of exposure. So, the energy actually delivered over a session is influenced by irradiance, distance, and duration.
Also, a small, highly concentrated device may deliver substantial light to a limited coverage area. At the same time, a larger panel is likely to distribute light across a larger part of your body.
Understanding what influences the coverage area can help you choose the right at-home RLT device such that it delivers an appropriate amount of light across the intended treatment area while remaining convenient and comfortable to use.
Build Quality Features That Separate Premium Devices From Basic Models
Here are some build quality features that separate premium RLT devices from basic models:
- Thermal management: LEDs and electronic components generate a lot of heat during use. Hence, thermal management with effective ventilation, heat sinks, fans, and other cooling systems is necessary to maintain reliable performance.
- Stable power supply: A reliable power supply can ensure consistent LED operation and might enhance the durability of the device.
- Optical design: Lenses and reflectors determine the beam angle, influence light distribution, and affect how evenly light reaches the treatment area.
- User-friendly controls: Intuitive controls can make it easier for you to operate your RLT device correctly and incorporate sessions into your regular routine easily.
- Electrical safety: It is important to choose a device with features that ensure electrical safety and protection.
- Flicker performance: Devices that minimize or eliminate LED flickers are likely to improve visual comfort, particularly during repeated or longer sessions.
How Professional Light Therapy Technology Is Moving Into Consumer Devices
The growing interest among consumers in improving their health through safe, non-invasive methods has led manufacturers to design and manufacture RLT devices that are easy to use, while preserving their quality and sophisticated engineering technologies.
This transition is also changing what consumers expect from their wellness products.
However, technical sophistication should not be confused with proven clinical effectiveness. A device having advanced LEDs and impressive engineering may not always produce a particular health outcome. Hence, consumers should be aware of how to distinguish between technical engineering terms and health claims so that they can choose the best device that meets their needs and expectations.
Final Thoughts
Clinical-grade home light therapy is less about one specific feature and more about the quality of multiple specifications, including accurate wavelength delivery, thoughtful dual-chip LED configurations, appropriate irradiance, controlled dosing, effective coverage, thermal management, and durable construction.
Being aware of what these specifications actually mean and how they influence your RLT sessions and results is the key to choosing the best device suitable for your specific health goals.

articles.title: 14 ans après le fiasco : Microsoft assure que Windows sur Arm est enfin prêt
articles.text:
Le 25 août, Microsoft a publié un billet déclarant Windows sur Arm « plateforme de premier plan pour n’importe quelle charge de travail ». NVIDIA, qui signe ici sa première incursion dans le marché des SoC pour PC Windows, livrera sa puce RTX Spark dans des machines de Microsoft, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo et MSI pour l’automne 2026. Quatorze ans après la Surface RT, c’est la troisième tentative de la firme de Redmond sur ce segment.
Du milliard perdu sur la Surface RT à la facture RTX Spark
La première tentative remonte à 2012, avec la Surface RT, une tablette Windows compilée pour Arm qui ne pouvait pas exécuter les applications x86 et se retrouvait cantonnée au Windows Store. Le bilan est brutal : une dépréciation de près d’un milliard de dollars sur les stocks invendus, et une réputation d’incompatibilité qui colle au segment pendant des années. Le Surface Pro X, sorti en 2019, parie sur l’émulation pour faire tourner les applications 32 bits, mais les performances s’effondrent à l’usage, et même Google Chrome souffre visiblement.
La troisième tentative arrive avec un partenaire jusqu’ici absent du marché des SoC PC. Le RTX Spark intègre un CPU Grace à 20 cœurs, un GPU Blackwell à 6 144 cœurs CUDA et jusqu’à 128 Go de mémoire unifiée, gravé en 3 nm chez TSMC. NVIDIA revendique des performances GPU comparables à une RTX 5070 de bureau dans un portable fin. La firme de Redmond avance que plus de 7 000 applications et jeux fonctionnent nativement sur la plateforme, chiffre issu du site Works on Windows on Arm. Les prix évoqués par Morgan Stanley dans une analyse de marché se situent entre 1 799 dollars pour les versions N1 d’entrée de gamme et 2 899 dollars minimum pour les machines N1X haut de gamme.
Ce que NVIDIA promet, ce que personne n’a encore mesuré
En France, l’actuel Surface Laptop 15 se négocie déjà entre 1 769 et 3 119 euros selon les configurations. Le Surface Laptop Ultra ira plus haut, sans que Microsoft ait communiqué un tarif ou une date de disponibilité précise pour le marché français. Pour qui projetait d’acheter un laptop haut de gamme cet automne, attendre les premiers tests indépendants vaut la peine d’être envisagé.
La promesse de faire tourner toutes les applications Windows repose sur Prism, l’émulateur qui traduit les instructions x86 vers Arm à la volée. C’était déjà la promesse centrale du Surface Pro X en 2019, avec le résultat qu’on sait. Les logiciels anti-triche posent une question supplémentaire que NVIDIA et Microsoft n’ont pas documentée : les joueurs qui espèrent lancer Valorant ou Fortnite sans accroc devront attendre les premiers retours terrain.
Cinq ans plus tôt, Apple avait relevé ce même défi avec la transition vers Apple Silicon, et Rosetta 2 avait rendu la bascule vers Arm transparente pour les utilisateurs Mac. Les MacBook Pro se vendent à des prix du même ordre que ceux évoqués pour le Surface Ultra. Microsoft arrive avec la même architecture unifiée, mais sans l’écosystème fermé qui avait permis à Apple de contrôler la compatibilité de bout en bout.

articles.title: African startups invited to apply for up to $1.5k from DIV Fund - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African tech startups have been invited to apply for up to US$1.5 million from the global DIV Fund.
The DIV Fund programme is open to innovations across multiple sectors, including health, agriculture, education, climate, and livelihoods. This flexibility allows a wide range of solutions addressing social and economic challenges to qualify.
The fund is structured across three stages. Early-stage ideas can receive up to US$200,000 under stage one to test and validate their concept; stage two supports scaling efforts with funding of up to US$500,000, and in exceptional cases up to US$750,000; and stage three provides up to US$1.5 million for solutions that are ready for large-scale expansion.
The fund is open globally, but supported projects must focus on improving lives in developing countries. Applications are open here until September 30.

articles.title: Lancé à près de 2 000 €, ce téléviseur OLED de Samsung coûte désormais moins de 800 €
articles.text:
Pas besoin de viser le téléviseur le plus cher du catalogue pour profiter des atouts de l’OLED. Sorti en 2025 à 1 999 €, le Samsung S90F occupe une place intermédiaire dans la gamme de la marque, sous le S95F et au-dessus du S85F. Son prix a depuis suffisamment baissé pour rendre ce 55 pouces bien plus accessible.
Chez Joybuy, cette version référencée TQ55S90F, descend à 799,99 € au lieu de 899 €, et la remise s’applique directement sur la page du produit, sans offre de remboursement à envoyer après coup.
Que vaut le Samsung S90F ?
Le S90F repose sur une dalle OLED de 55 pouces en définition 4K (3840 x 2160 pixels). Concrètement, chaque pixel produit sa propre lumière et peut s’éteindre totalement. À l’écran, cela se traduit par des noirs parfaits et un excellent contraste, particulièrement appréciables pour regarder un film dans une pièce sombre. Les sous-titres ou les étoiles sur un ciel noir s’affichent ainsi sans les halos lumineux que peuvent parfois laisser apparaître les écrans LCD.
Samsung place ce modèle un cran en dessous de son S95F, plus lumineux. Le S90F reste néanmoins bien équipé pour le jeu, un terrain où Samsung soigne ses téléviseurs depuis plusieurs générations. La contrepartie à connaître avant d’acheter : comme tous les téléviseurs Samsung, le S90F fait l’impasse sur le Dolby Vision et se limite au HDR10+. En pratique, selon les plateformes et les films que vous regardez, cette absence peut passer totalement inaperçue.
À ce prix, le Samsung S90F est-il une bonne affaire ?
Les 1 200 € de baisse font forcément leur effet, mais ce Samsung n’est plus un téléviseur à 2 000 € depuis longtemps. Les fabricants renouvellent leurs gammes chaque année, avec des tarifs de lancement élevés et des nouveautés souvent modestes. Les prix fondent bien plus vite que les écrans ne vieillissent.
Le tarif habituel est plutôt autour de 1 000 € aujourd’hui, ce qui rend la baisse tout de même intéressante. Ce Samsung fait partie des excellents rapports qualité-prix, aussi convaincant pour les films que pour le jeu. De quoi profiter de GTA 6 dans de très bonnes conditions en novembre prochain.

articles.title: Govt notifies Rs 1,27,500-cr Semicon 2.0
articles.text:
Govt notifies Rs 1,27,500-cr Semicon 2.0
The move comes at a time when semiconductors have emerged as a critical strategic resource globally, with the AI boom driving unprecedented demand for advanced chips and memory.
The government on Monday notified the Semicon 2.0 scheme, setting in motion the Rs 1,27,500-crore plan that seeks to deepen India's semiconductor ambitions--from chip manufacturing to a full-stack ecosystem encompassing indigenous design and IP, equipment, materials, advanced packaging, R&D and talent development.
The move comes at a time when semiconductors have emerged as a critical strategic resource globally, with the AI boom driving unprecedented demand for advanced chips and memory. At the same time, growing concerns over supply-chain vulnerabilities and shifting geopolitics have pushed global players to expand semiconductor capacities and reduce dependence on concentrated production hubs.
The Semicon 2.0 scheme was approved by the Union Cabinet on July 15, 2026. The notification on Monday spells out the contours of the new programme detailing how the Rs 1,27,500-crore outlay will be implemented, and how incentives will be structured, and the eligibility criteria for various categories.
"Now the time is ripe to move to next stage to develop semiconducor ecosystem through Semicon 2.0. The objective of the scheme is self reliance and fostering a globally competitive industry," IT Secretary S Krishnan said at a briefing.
For design of chips for commercial sector, the eligibility will be startups, and companies owned by Indian citizens or OCI.
For startups, financial support will be in the form of grant and equity co-investment, and for companies it would be in the form of royalty financing or equity co-investment.
When it comes to setting up more fabs, the new scheme will provide 40% fiscal support for silicon fabs and 35% for compound, display (LCD, OLED, micro LED), and other specialised fabs.
For strengthening ATMP/OSAT, (Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging/Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test), it supports advanced and legacy packaging with an incentive of 35% of capex for advanced packaging and 25% of capex for conventional packaging.
Previously, under the first phase of the programme, the government had approved 12 semiconductor projects across six states, with three facilities--Micron's ATMP plant, Kaynes Semicon and CG Semi OSAT facility--having commenced commercial production earlier this year.

articles.title: Cuál es el valor en el mercado de la criptomoneda ethereum este día
articles.text:
Ethereum es una plataforma digital que adopta la tecnología de cadena de bloques (blockchain) y expande su uso a una gran variedad de aplicaciones, mientras que ether es su criptomoneda nativa. En el mundo de las finanzas digitales es común que la criptomoneda sea llamada como la red, aunque en realidad no son lo mismo.
La plataforma ethereum, creada en el 2015 por el programador Vitalik Buterin, buscaba ser un instrumento para aplicaciones descentralizadas y colaborativas sobre las que se pueden hacer contratos inteligentes (dAPPs)
PUBLICIDAD
Al igual que el bitcoin, el valor de ether se disparó en un corto periodo de tiempo. En enero de 2016, ether cotizaba alrededor de un dólar y actualmente tiene un máximo histórico de 4.953,73 dólares.
El costo de la criptomoneda de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2474.5 dólares por unidad.
Esto quiere decir que el activo digital tuvo un cambio del 1.59 el último día, así como una variación del 0.0 % en los últimos 60 minutos.
PUBLICIDAD
Actualmente, ethereum se encuentra en el lugar #2 de popularidad en el mercado digital. Cabe mencionar que el máximo histórico que ha alcanzado esta criptodivisa es de 4891.7 dólares por unidad.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum 2.0: las claves
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
PUBLICIDAD
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
PUBLICIDAD
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: South African VC Mamor Capital raises $18.8 million first fund
articles.text:
For South African startups, getting customers is only half the battle. Even after people start paying for their products, raising enough money to grow can remain difficult. That is the funding gap Mamor Capital Ventures wants to target with its first venture capital fund.
The black women-owned and managed firm has raised R300 million ($18.8 million) in the first close of its inaugural fund, with the Public Investment Corporation (PIC), South Africa’s largest asset manager, as its anchor investor.
Mamor is still raising towards its R550 million ($34.375 million) target and says it will invest in South African technology companies that already have paying customers.
Mamor’s fund points to a bigger problem in South Africa’s startup market, where companies can have paying customers and a working business yet still struggle to find investors willing to fund their next stage of growth.
Mamokete Ramathe, founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Mamor Capital, revealed that the firm spent more than three years raising the fund and found that many traditional investors, including pension funds and banks, remain cautious about venture capital.
Some investors, she said, have mandates or risk limits that make it difficult to invest in early-stage companies. Others still associate venture capital with backing businesses that have not yet proved that their products work.
“The fundraising journey reinforced that institutional appetite for venture capital in South Africa is still developing,” Ramathe told TechCabal in an interview on Monday.
Mamor is trying to reduce some of that risk by investing in companies that have already shown that customers will pay for their products or services. Ramathe said the firm does not require companies to be profitable before investing. Instead, it looks at whether they have paying customers, can retain them, have a market they can grow into, and have a realistic path to becoming profitable.
Southern Africa’s VC market recorded R13.35 billion ($834.4 million) in active investments across 1,325 deals in 2024, but limited exits and follow-on funding remain barriers. That puts Mamor in a market where capital is growing, while some founders still struggle to secure the next round.
She explained that a company may have moved beyond an idea and built a business, but still be too small or risky for a bank loan. At the same time, the market still has gaps in follow-on funding, with limited exits and funding for later-stage companies remaining a challenge
“There is a significant funding gap for early-stage, post-revenue businesses in South Africa,” Ramathe said.
Fuzlin Levy-Hassen, Mamor’s co-founder and chief financial officer (CFO), said the fund will focus on businesses with evidence of genuine demand rather than simply promising future growth.
“We are looking for businesses that have moved beyond proving an idea and can show real commercial demand,” Levy-Hassen said.
The fund will focus on areas including financial access, digital infrastructure and technology that Mamor believes can expand economic participation by helping more people and businesses access financial services and markets.
The PIC’s investment is significant because institutional investors have traditionally been cautious about putting money into venture capital, where returns can take years, and some investments can fail.
Leon Smit, the PIC’s acting chief investment officer, said the backing gives the organisation exposure to South Africa’s growing venture capital market while supporting transformation.
“Mamor Capital brings together an experienced investment team, a clear strategy, and a strong transformation proposition,” Smit said.
The PIC also believes institutional investors can play a bigger role in providing the long-term capital needed to develop South Africa’s venture capital market. There are signs that interest is growing. Ramathe said some institutions that are not yet investing are researching venture capital and looking at ways to participate in parts of the market where the risks are lower.
Ketso Gordhan, CEO of the South African Small and Medium Enterprise Fund, which invested through its High Impact Seed Fund of Funds, an early-stage venture capital investment vehicle, said increasing the number of local fund managers able to back technology businesses is important.
“Our investment is intended to strengthen the pool of local fund managers with the capability to identify and support promising technology businesses,” noted Gordhan.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Más de 12 TB de juegos y betas nunca vistas de Steam se han filtrado en internet: y no ha sido un hackeo
articles.text:
Este fin de semana Steam ha sufrido quizás la mayor filtración de toda su historia. Y es que tal y como han recogido distintos medios, se han recopilado más de 12 TB de archivos procedentes de la plataforma de Valve. En esos archivos podemos encontrar juegos sin publicar, prototipos, versiones preliminares y otros datos procedentes de Steam entre 2003 y 2013. Pero igual “filtración” no es el término más preciso para este caso, pues la información se encontraba “a plena vista”.
Qué ha pasado. El conocido como “Steam Teraleak”, lleva ya días circulando por redes y su creador lo describe como un volcado casi completo de los antiguos servidores de contenido “Steam2” de Steam, la infraestructura que Valve utilizaba antes de cambiar al sistema actual SteamPipe en 2013. Según cuentan desde Ars Technica, la filtración abarca miles de “depots” individuales, esencialmente cada versión de cada juego que jamás se acabaron subiendo a los servidores actuales, incluidos títulos de la propia Valve y de editoras de terceros que distribuyeron sus juegos a Steam a lo largo de esos años.
No ha sido un hackeo. Tanto el conocido dataminer ‘Valve Gabe Follower’ como el streamer y analista ‘Valve Scolcer’ afirmaron en redes sociales que los archivos se extrajeron a través de un punto de acceso de una API públicamente accesible y que no requería credenciales de ningún tipo.
Scolcer contaba que los datos estaban “Oculto a simple vista, pero sin ninguna protección”. Eso explica también por qué la filtración se detiene en 2013, ya que fue justo en ese año cuando Valve retiró el sistema antiguo de Steam.
En detalle. Hay toda una montaña de datos, así que la comunidad ya está manos a la obra clasificando toda la información. Además, los datos correspondientes a los juegos de Valve están dejando cosas bastante interesantes. Y es que han aparecido múltiples versiones nunca vistas y jugables de Portal 2 que revelan diálogos descartados de GLaDOS, modelos de armas que no se llegaron a incluir como el “Weaponizer”, secuencias alternativas y mucho más.
El archivo también contiene una versión de principios de 2008 de Left 4 Dead con una interfaz diferente y líneas de diálogos nunca vistos, material en fase alfa de Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, que muestra una interfaz más al estilo de Source, y recursos de F-Stop, un spin-off descartado de Portal basado en una cámara. Más allá del catálogo de Valve, los dataminers también han encontrado prototipos y betas de títulos como Dragon Age: Origins, Batman: Arkham Asylum, Spore, Mirror's Edge, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines, Sonic the Hedgehog 4, y mucho más.
Entre líneas. El hecho de que la filtración incluya tanto material de terceros también plantea algunas inquietudes. Y es que tal y como cuenta Tyler McVicker, veterano de la industria y experto en la actualidad de Valve, advertía en redes sociales que manipular el archivo es legalmente arriesgado precisamente porque no es solo contenido propio de Valve, calificando la situación de “drásticamente más peligrosa” que una simple filtración de alguna versión interna, y sugiriendo a la gente alejarse de estos archivos por si acaso. La comunidad de Valve Cut Content contaba a Ars Technica que creen que los archivos podrían haber sido recopilados en privado durante años antes de ser finalmente compilados y publicados en un solo paquete, en lugar de haberse extraído desde los servidores de Valve recientemente.
Qué es lo siguiente. Valve no ha emitido ninguna declaración pública sobre la filtración hasta el momento. Además, dada la antigüedad de los archivos (pues el material más reciente tiene ya más de una década) es poco probable que represente un problema de seguridad grave para la empresa, pero aun así expone un fragmento enorme de la historia del videojuego en PC que muchos entusiastas valorarán. Además de que es información que, hasta que se categorice y se analice con calma, habrá cuerda para rato. Y es que no será nada raro ver durante estos días y meses nueva información sobre el tema.

articles.title: GTA 6 provoque une ruée sur la PS5 : les stocks fondent, les prix s'envolent
articles.text:
GTA 6 provoque une ruée sur la PS5 : les stocks fondent, les prix s'envolent
Depuis la diffusion de 27 minutes de gameplay sur Netflix le 27 août, la PS5 Pro est en rupture chez la majorité des revendeurs américains. En Europe, les stocks se tendent et les prix grimpent parfois au-delà des 1 000 euros.
Il aura suffi d'une demi-heure de gameplay capturé sur PlayStation 5 pour déclencher la panique. Depuis la diffusion de l'Extended Look de Grand Theft Auto VI sur Netflix, jeudi 27 août, la PS5 Pro s'arrache à un rythme que Sony n'avait probablement pas anticipé. Aux États-Unis, Best Buy, Target, Walmart et Amazon affichent tous des stocks épuisés. Seul le PlayStation Direct de Sony maintenait encore un inventaire limité au tarif officiel de 899 dollars au 29 août.
Des revendeurs tiers qui flairent l'aubaine
Sur les marketplaces américaines, les vendeurs tiers ont immédiatement gonflé leurs tarifs. Les annonces oscillent entre 1 100 et 1 300 dollars selon Notebookcheck et Tech4Gamers, soit un surcoût de plus de 400 dollars par rapport au prix conseillé.
En Allemagne, le phénomène prend la même tournure : les comparateurs de prix affichent des offres qui démarrent autour de 999 euros pour une console vendue 899,99 euros, et certaines annonces Amazon.de mentionnent des délais d'expédition de trois à sept mois. MediaMarkt et Saturn signalent également des ruptures. En France, plusieurs revendeurs connaissent des tensions sur les stocks selon le site JustJeuxVideo, même si l'ampleur exacte de la pénurie reste difficile à mesurer sans données officielles.
Le paradoxe mérite d'être souligné : Rockstar n'a montré que du gameplay capturé sur PS5 standard lors de sa démonstration. GTA 6 figure bien comme titre "PS5 Pro Enhanced" sur le PlayStation Store, mais les détails techniques de cette version restent inconnus.
La crise mémoire amplifie le phénomène
La frénésie GTA 6 n'explique pas tout. La pénurie mondiale de composants DRAM, alimentée par la demande colossale des infrastructures d'IA, pèse sur les capacités de production de consoles depuis le début de l'année 2026. La combinaison d'une offre contrainte et d'une demande dopée par le jeu le plus attendu de la décennie crée un goulet d'étranglement que les scalpers exploitent sans vergogne.
GTA VI sortira le 19 novembre 2026 exclusivement en téléchargement, sur PS5 et Xbox Series X/S. Selon les estimations de Newzoo, les précommandes auraient généré environ 260 millions de dollars en première semaine à l'échelle mondiale. La situation pourrait encore s'intensifier à mesure que la date de lancement approche.

articles.title: Boston Dynamics' Spot robot dogs could soon be working with ICE in a $2 million deal
articles.text:
A hot potato: Spot, the robotic quadruped from Boston Dynamics, has been used in numerous professions over the years, but its most controversial application could be on the way. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is set to spend $2 million on the robot dogs, which could support officers by remotely assessing environments before they enter.
A new Department of Homeland Security procurement notice describes the possible purchase of Boston Dynamics SPOT robots and accessories valued at between $1 million and $2 million.
The document lists the robots' potential uses as inspection, situational awareness, and hazard assessment in environments that may pose risks to personnel.
It adds that these capabilities helps improve officer safety, supports informed operational decision-making, and enhances DHS's ability to respond to incidents involving dangerous, confined, unstable, or difficult-to-access areas.
Also read: Hyundai wants to sell humanoid and robot dogs through its car dealerships
There's no mention of the robots being used to apprehend people or make arrests, which was later confirmed by a senior DHS official speaking to NBC News, though that's unlikely to make their use by ICE any less controversial.
This won't be the first time Spot has been used by a government agency. In 2019, the Massachusetts State Police bomb squad leased one of the robots for use as a "mobile remote observation device." It was sent to inspect suspicious objects and dangerous locations, taking part in at least two incidents.
The NYPD later deployed a heavily modified Spot known as Digidog. The robot was used for reconnaissance during a 2020 incident in which a gunman barricaded himself inside a basement, and again the following year to investigate a house during a reported home invasion before officers entered.
Digidog reportedly completed around six missions without harming civilians, but footage of the robot in action prompted a backlash over surveillance and the increasingly Black Mirror-like appearance of modern policing. The NYPD terminated its $94,000 lease in 2021, only to bring Digidog back two years later. The department acquired two of the robots for $750,000, saying they would only be deployed in life-threatening situations such as bomb threats.
Spot also has a history with the US military. An early version was tested by the Marines as a potential load-carrying and ground-reconnaissance platform. While it was much quieter than Boston Dynamics' gas-powered AlphaDog, Spot had to be monitored continuously and could carry only around 40 pounds of equipment. Those limitations meant the military ultimately shelved the project.
Boston Dynamics prohibits customers from using Spot to harm or intimidate people, warning that it will take "appropriate measures to mitigate that misuse." Even if it believes this doesn't apply to ICE, the company will have to decide whether up to $2 million in sales will be worth the bad publicity.

articles.title: Inside Meta’s push to put robots to work in data centers
articles.text:
Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.
Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”
At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.
Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II, and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.
But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don’t have a chance to do this,” he said.
Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry, they sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.
Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.
“More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things,” says Paul Golding, who oversees so-called physical intelligence at the chipmaker Analog Devices.
The growing use of robots has received little attention from the activists driving a powerful nationwide movement against data centers. Tech companies often tout jobs for humans as an upside to the developments that can be used to justify tax breaks for them. In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates what is now its largest data center campus, which employs hundreds of workers. The company opened the facility in 2014 and has several years left of a property tax break that allows it to save tens of millions of dollars annually, which the city has viewed as a worthwhile trade-off for having its cachet upped by having Meta jobs.
In Altoona, Meta worker group chats have taken on a demoralized tone, “saying we’re all going to be gone in a few years anyway because of the robots,” a person familiar with the discussions says. Even if adoption of robots proves slower than anticipated, some worry the quality of jobs available is trending downward. Two of the workers say that Meta is developing AI software and other technologies that they believe will allow it to hire lower-skilled—and thus, lower-paid—workers and centralize some roles in areas like Denver, Colorado, that are more financially advantageous to the company.
“They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting,” one Meta data center worker says. “They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.”
Meta contends its need for skilled workers remains robust. This year, the company launched a long-term program to train thousands of people annually from any background in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing work at no cost to them. Meta is even guaranteeing employment in states such as Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas for those who complete the training. It also partnered with building trade unions to fund apprenticeship programs.
But as communities rethink data center tax breaks and weigh putting new rules on the industry, the prospect of robots replacing at least some jobs may need to become a bigger concern. Altoona Mayor Dean O’Connor tells WIRED he hasn’t given much thought to robots taking jobs at Meta’s data center, though he frames automation as inevitable. “We will deal with it as it comes,” he says.
Tripping cables
In a 2023 YouTube video, Meta touted that it was using a self-driving tugger robot to transport heavy server racks within its data centers as well as a wheeled, barcode-reading robot developed in-house to track inventory. The next year, Microsoft and Google unveiled separate investments in robots for their data center operations, and Amazon last year discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
Pursuing robotics for “economically valuable tasks,” like “replacing a faulty server rack,” is “absolutely something we’re looking into at Microsoft,” Ashley Llorens, a managing director for the company’s research accelerator, tells WIRED.
Meta’s tugger and inventory robots are now operating in a number of the company’s data centers, including in Iowa and Virginia, according to the people familiar with the projects. They say the robots generally work well, though there are limitations.
The inventory bot is now also being used for failure inspections, but it can’t differentiate between green and red indicator lights on equipment because its camera only detects grayscale, meaning human checks are still required to assess some breakdowns. The device also struggles with corners and traversing the cables that are often in the path of its wheels. Because there aren’t that many of them, the robots need to be moved between buildings, which requires a door-opening human who maneuvers the robot with a remote control.
Two sources also describe the inventory bot as too slow. One says Meta previously explored using drones as a faster alternative but ultimately didn’t pursue the idea.
Inside the testbed
The Altoona data center campus is often where Meta prototypes new technologies. “What they do here in Altoona, they take to their other sites and put that in place there,” says O’Connor.
Since last June, Meta has been trying out a pair of dual-armed Watney robots for some cabling work at one of its Altoona buildings, according to one of the people familiar with the company’s efforts. The robots are supervised by humans and can’t work as fast as people yet, but they show promise.
After Watney launched in 2023, it put out a demo of a laundry-folding robot that it claimed could also handle janitorial work inside businesses. The San Francisco startup quietly pivoted to data center robots early last year, according to archived copies of its website.
Meta is testing additional robots in New Albany, Ohio, at the company’s newest data center campus known as Prometheus. Four-wheel robots “with a scissor-lift-style riser and a six-axis arm on top” made by the automation giant ABB are being used there to reseat parts and, eventually, they may take on other tasks with diminishing human oversight, a person familiar with the product says.
But the idea that robots will prevail over humans isn’t guaranteed. “There’s been a lot of pilots and demos, but no provable working solution,” says Helen Oleynikova, CEO of Exclaim Robotics, which is developing prototypes to replace broken parts and reset cables in data centers.
At Meta’s data centers, some workers have complained about the amount of downtime the robots need to recharge their batteries, according to the people familiar with the matter. Meta has also acknowledged internally that robots aren’t equipped for certain tasks, such as the intense cabling work required to run an Nvidia GB300 supercomputer. “Things have been designed for human hands forever to make everything a five-minute repair,” says one former Meta employee. “Redesigning everything will take time.” But the robots are getting prepared.
Wired.com is your essential daily guide to what's next, delivering the most original and complete take you'll find anywhere on innovation's impact on technology, science, business and culture.

articles.title: The Terra Kaffe Aero is a barista's dream, making hot and cold milk froth, and even matcha at the press of a button
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Terra Kaffe Aero makes it quick and easy to whip up your milk of choice as a cold foam, hot froth, or hot milk. There's even a dedicated matcha setting, which is a quicker and easier way to make matcha than with a bamboo whisk.
Pros
- +Easy to use and clean up
- +Four settings: Hot Froth, Hot Milk, Cold Foam, and Matcha
- +Elegant style
- +Effective
Cons
- -Pricey
- -Takes up more space than a handheld frother
Why you can trust TechRadar
Terra Kaffe Aero: two-minute review
The Terra Kaffe Aero does what it does well. There are four settings: Cold Foam, Hot Froth, Hot Milk, and Matcha. Just spin the dial and press it to make your selection. In just a few minutes, your beverage will be ready to drink. Cleaning it is super easy, just remove the whisk and hand-wash it, the pitcher, and the lid.
I found that all of the settings worked well. I tested each of the milk settings with skim milk which worked great. I also tested them all with a barista-style pistachio milk which came highly recommended in my research, and that also worked really well. I did try a low-calorie almond milk (not specifically made for frothing, and not recommended, but I had it in the house) and that was a fail, though I can't blame the Aero for that.
I made matcha in the Aero several different ways. Though I'm new to matcha, I thought it turned out just as yummy as the $7 matcha latte I got at my local coffee and tea shop.
Just for kicks, I also made a simple salad dressing. I just put together some olive oil and balsamic vinegar and used the Cold Foam setting. The Terra Kaffe Aero emulsified the dressing beautifully.
If you're looking for a dedicated pitcher-style frother, I don't know how you could really do better than the Terra Kaffe Aero.
Terra Kaffe Aero: price and availability
- Available at Amazon and on Terra Kaffe's website
- Retails for $149.95 (£110.73 GBP/$210.85 AUD)
- Choose Matte Black or Stainless Steel
The Terra Kaffe Aero milk frother is currently available on Amazon and on Terra Kaffe's own website. The retail price is $149.95 (£110.73 GBP/$210.85 AUD). It comes in two different colorways, Matte Black or Stainless Steel, though both color options refer only to the pitcher itself. The base is matte black on both models.
Terra Kaffe Aero: specs
| Terra Kaffe Aero specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Name | Terra Kaffe Aero | 
| Heated temperature range | 140°F–160°F | 
| Dimensions | Carafe: 4.3” (H) x 3.8” (Diameter) Base: 4.2” (W) x 2.4” (H) x 4.2” (Diameter) | 
| Carafe material | Stainless steel, glass, silicone, and plastic | 
| Settings | Cold Foam, Hot Froth, Hot Milk, Matcha | 
| Volume | 6.7 oz (Hot Froth), 13.5 oz (Hot Milk) | 
| Compatible milk types | Dairy, oat, almond, soy, and more (ideally, choose a "Barista" style) | 
Terra Kaffe Aero: design
- Attractive and simple design
- Interchangeable whisks for milk or matcha
- Four settings
The Terra Kaffe Aero is an elegantly designed multi-use milk frother. It's nice-looking and it's something you won't mind having out on your kitchen counter.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The Aero comes with two different whisks, one for milk and one for matcha. Place your whisk of choice in the bottom of the pitcher until it clicks into place. Add your liquid, the minimum and maximum fill lines are clearly printed on the inside. Place the lid on top and the pitcher on the base. Spin the dial on the base until you get to the one you want and then press it. The base is magnetized, which is how it controls the whisk from inside the pitcher. Progress lights show you how your beverage is coming along and a series of beeps let you know it's complete.
There is a "hidden" settings menu on the Terra Kaffe Aero. To access it, turn the dial to select the drink setting you wish to adjust. Double click the dial (press twice within .7 seconds) to enter that drink's settings menu. The selected drink will flash and the current setting will be indicated by the number of LED lights. For the Hot Milk and Matcha settings, turn the dial to adjust the temperature. For the Cold Foam and Hot Froth settings, turning the dial will adjust the amount of froth.
- Design score: 4.5/5
Terra Kaffe Aero: performance
- Couldn't be easier to use
- Takes just over three minutes
- Beautiful foam from both dairy and plant milk
I put the Terra Kaffe Aero through its paces, and overall I think it did a great job. The foams held up nicely, even after stirring. I tested each of the settings, Cold Foam, Hot Froth, Hot Milk, and Matcha several times. I tried out both dairy milk and plant milk, and learned some things along the way.
Hot froth (dairy milk)
I prefer skim milk, so that's what I used. A dairy milk with a bit of fat in it will likely foam up even better, but I was happy with the results I got using skim. Surprisingly, whole milk and cream are not the best milks for frothing, as they have too much fat. Two percent is the ideal frothing milk.
I started with the Hot Froth setting, pouring in skim milk up to the minimum fill line. I thought the foam was just lovely, as you can see in my series of photos below. The foam held up fine to stirring.

Cold foam (dairy milk)
The Cold Foam setting with skim milk also came out great. It's perfect for iced coffee and other cold beverages.

Hot milk (dairy milk)
The Hot Milk setting with skim milk turned out fine, though it perhaps produced more foam than I was expecting. If you hate foam and just want the milk hot, you're better off using a different method of heating your milk. If you don't mind a bit of foam, this will work for you.

Plant-based milks
First I tried frothing a random low-calorie almond milk I had in the house. Don't bother with this. After that complete fail, I did some research about the best plant-based milks for frothing, and the one I had just tried was at the bottom of the barrel.
There are a few exceptions, but the easiest way to choose a plant milk that will froth properly is to pick one that says "barista" right on the label. The barista milks are made for frothing and they have enough fat (or gums or other additives) to do so. I chose a barista-labeled pistachio milk without gums but with a good amount of fat in it. I picked this one for its mild, milky flavor, but you could also use other nut milks or soy, oat, or pea milk. As long as it says barista on the label, you're good to go. If you can't find one with the barista labeling, at least look for a full-fat plant milk. Oat and soy are supposed to be particularly good for this.
I used the barista-style plant milk to make both hot froth and cold foam several times. It worked really well, in fact it was just about the same as the dairy milk.

Matcha
I had never actually had matcha before, so my son suggested that I try one a coffee/tea shop before reviewing the Terra Kaffe Aero. That way I'd know what it's "supposed" to taste like before making it myself. I did so and was pleasantly surprised to find that I liked it. I don't really like green tea or even black tea all that much, but matcha has more of a mild taste in my opinion.
Matcha is traditionally made with a fair amount of equipment, including a sieve and a bamboo whisk. Enthusiasts will also use a scale to measure out the amount of matcha powder and water with precision.
I made matcha in the Terra Kaffe Aero a bunch of times, using instructions I found online specifically for using a milk frother as opposed to using all of the "proper" equipment. I purchased some ceremonial-grade (which is a higher grade than culinary) matcha powder, which came with a measuring scoop. I used that for measuring the powder rather than a scale. I did not sift the powder through a sieve, though my results might have been better if I had: I usually had a bit of powder at the bottom of my cup.
At any rate, I found two different basic recommended methods in my research: make the matcha in water and then add milk, or make the matcha directly in the milk. I found I preferred the former method, because the latter resulted in a too-milky beverage for my taste. However, both methods worked just fine in the Terra Kaffe Auto.
I will note that I did get a bit of powder left at the bottom of my matcha drinks. So it's not a perfect system, but it's a heck of a lot easier than doing it the traditional way.

And more
Just for fun, I decided to make a simple salad dressing. I don't know about you, but I hate salad dressings where the oil and vinegar elements are separated. I prefer my dressings totally emulsified. So, I poured a bit of olive oil and balsamic vinegar into the Aero and started the Cold Foam cycle. Not that I was looking for foam, but I definitely didn't want it hot. The results: a perfectly emulsified and delicious salad dressing. There was a tiny bit of foam but it disappeared when I poured it onto my salad.

- Performance score: 4.5/5
Should you buy the Terra Kaffe Aero?
| Terra Kaffe Aero score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | It's probably better than a hand-held battery-operated whisk, but it's also far more expensive | 4/5 | 
| Design | The Aero is aesthetically pleasing and cleverly designed. | 4.5/5 | 
| Performance | It performed well with both plant and dairy milk, matcha, and more. | 4.5/5 | 
Buy it if
You want a one-touch frother
You don't want to put in the extra effort to froth your milk with a frothing wand or hand frother. Just dial and press.
You want to make matcha without all the accoutrements
No need to buy (and often replace) a bamboo whisk and the other matcha tools. Just scoop your matcha powder into water or milk, select the Matcha setting, and press.
You want something attractive you can leave on the counter
Beautify your coffee station at home with the Terra Kaffe Aero. You won't want to hide it away.
Don't buy it if
It's out of budget
You're paying for the convenience, functionality, and aesthetics here. While a hand-held battery-operated whisk frother is a bit more hit-or-miss, it's exponentially cheaper.
You're a matcha-making expert
If you already have the whole matcha setup at home and the routine (or should I say ritual) down pat, the Aero version of matcha may not do it for you.
You just don't want another appliance
While this isn't a large machine, it is another appliance you'll need to devote space (and an outlet) to in your kitchen.
Terra Kaffe Aero: also consider
Smeg Mini Milk Frother
This little beauty come in a number of colors. It makes hot froth, cold foam, and hot milk. It does take up less space on the counter than the Terra Kaffe Aero.
Read our Smeg Mini Milk Frother review
Philips Baristina Milk Frother
It's a bit cheaper and smaller than the Terra Kaffe Aero. It makes hot milk, hot foam, and cold foam. Choose from two colors, black or white.
Check out our Philips Baristina Milk Frother review
How I tested the Terra Kaffe Aero
I tested all of the settings: Hot Froth, Hot Milk, Cold Foam, and Matcha multiple times. I tested skim dairy milk and two different plant-based milks. I made matcha in water and tried it straight, added frothed milk to it, and made the matcha directly in milk. I tested it both hot and iced. I also made a simple salad dressing on the Cold Foam setting.
First reviewed August 2026
